parole.significato: A verb-building suffix that can be added to nouns or adjectives.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -a, from Old Norse -a, from Proto-Germanic *-ōną.
From Old Norse -andi, from Proto-Germanic *-andz, from Proto-Indo-European *-onts.

parole.significato: Regular construction of comparative: ful (“ugly”) → fulare (“uglier”)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -are, from Old Norse -ari (also substituting Old Norse -ir), from Proto-Germanic *-ōzô.

parole.significato: creates superlative of an adjective, if the noun comes before the adjective, and the noun is in indefinite singular for…
parole.testo: From Old Norse -astr, from Proto-Germanic *-ōstaz.

parole.significato: Used to form the names of residents or inhabitants of particular places, in particular towns/cities.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -boe, from Old Norse búi, from Proto-Germanic *būô.

parole.significato: Suffix for definite form singular of common gender nouns which end in a consonant, e.g. fisk (“fish”) + -en → fisken (“…
parole.testo: From forms of Old Norse hinn (demonstrative pronoun), suffixed to the end of the noun stem. From Old Norse -inn, -in, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz, from Proto-Indo-European *i-.

From Old Swedish -falder, from Old Norse -faldr, from Proto-Germanic *-falþaz. Cognate with Danish -fold. The noun suffix is a calque of German -falt, as in Einfalt (“simplicity, simple-mindedness”), equivalent to -faldighet, as in trefaldighet (“trinity, threefoldness”).

parole.significato: Used to form verbal nouns from verbs; -ation; -ing
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish -ing, -ung, from Old Norse -ing, -ung, from Proto-Germanic *-ingō, *-ungō. Cognate with German -ung.

parole.significato: added to a noun stem, causing i-mutation (if applicable), forming a noun denoting an inhabitant or original of a partic…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -inger, from Old Norse -ingr, from Proto-Germanic *-ingaz. Cognate with Icelandic -ingur, English -ing (derivative suffix).

parole.significato: -ish, of or pertaining to; making an adjective based on a noun
parole.testo: From Old Norse -iskr, from Proto-Germanic *-iskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *-iskos.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns from adjectives
parole.testo: From Old Norse -ka, from Proto-Germanic *-ukōną, *-ikōną.

parole.significato: used to create nouns from adjectives.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -lēker, -leeker, from Old Norse -leikr, from Proto-Germanic *-laikaz.
Derived from Old Swedish -līker, from Old Norse -ligr, -líkr, Proto-Germanic *-līkaz. Cognate with Icelandic -legur, Faroese -ligur, Norwegian Nynorsk -leg, Danish -lig and Norwegian Bokmål -lig.

parole.significato: -en; Used with some adjectives or verbal stems to form inchoative verbs
parole.testo: From Old Norse -na, from Proto-Germanic *-naną.

parole.significato: Forms the comparative degree of a few adjectives, most of which change their stem vowel (umlaut) when this happens.
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse -ri, derived from Proto-Germanic *-izô.

parole.significato: Used to form the passive voice of verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse -sk, a grammaticalisation of Proto-Germanic *sek (reflexive pronoun).

parole.significato: -some; creating adjectives, mostly out of nouns
parole.testo: From Old Norse -samr, from Proto-Germanic *-samaz, a suffix form of *samaz (“same”).
From Old Norse -skapr, from Proto-Germanic *-skapiz.
From late Old Swedish adherton (earlier attartan), from Old Norse átján, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun.

From Old Swedish aptan, aftan, afton, from Old Norse aptann, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi. Cognates include Norwegian Nynorsk aftan, Norwegian Bokmål aften, Danish aften, Icelandic aftann, English even (evening), Dutch avond and German Abend.

From Old Norse aga (“to threaten”), from Proto-Germanic *agaz (“fear, dread”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʰ- (“to be depressed, afraid”). Cognates include Ancient Greek ἄχος (ákhos, “distress, pain”), English ey and awe.

From Old Norse agn, from Proto-Germanic *aganą (“bait”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱH-ono-, same source as Sanskrit अश्नाति (aśnāti, “to eat”), Sanskrit अशन (aśana, “eating”), Ancient Greek ἄκολος (ákolos, “morsel”).
From Old Norse ǫgn, from Proto-Germanic *ahanō.

From Old Swedish al, from Old Norse ǫlr (compare Icelandic elri, Danish el, Norwegian older), from Proto-Germanic *aluz, *alusō (compare English alder), variant of *alizō, *alisō (compare Dutch els, German Erle), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisos.
From Old Swedish alder, from Old Norse allr, from Proto-Germanic *allaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-.
From Old Norse almr, from Proto-Germanic *elmaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem.

parole.significato: elf; a human-resembling, often magical, being
parole.testo: From Old Norse alfr, from Proto-Germanic *albiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós.
Inherited from Old Norse ǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *anadz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts (“duck”).

parole.significato: to breathe (repeatedly draw air into, and expel it from, the lungs)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish anda, from Old Norse anda (“to breathe”), from Proto-Germanic *anadōną, having changed form from an active to a deponent verb.
From Old Swedish ande, from Old Norse andi, from Proto-Germanic *anadô.
From Old Swedish anlæt, anleth, anlit, ænlite, ænlæte, anlitte, andlite, anlite, from Old Norse andlit, Proto-Germanic *andawlitją. Cognate with Old English andwlite, German Antlitz.

parole.significato: other, (idiomatically, sometimes) else, (when not used as a determiner) (an)other one
parole.testo: From Old Swedish annar (accusative annan), from Old Norse annarr, from Proto-Germanic *anþeraz, from Proto-Indo-European *ánteros.
From Old Norse andsvar, from and- (“against, opposing”) and svar (“answer, reply”) (Proto-Germanic *andaswarō). Compare with English answer.
From Old Swedish apa, from Old Norse api, from Proto-Germanic *apô (“monkey, ape”), from Proto-Indo-European *abō- (“ape”).
From Old Swedish argher, from Old Norse argr, from Proto-Germanic *argaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃orǵʰ-, *h₃erǵʰ- (“to copulate”).
From Old Norse árla, from Old Norse ár, from Proto-Germanic *airi. Related to English early.
From Old Norse armr (“arm”), from Proto-Germanic *armaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ermos, *h₂ŕ̥mos.
From Old Norse armr (“poor”), from Proto-Germanic *armaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ormos.
From earlier almboge after influence from arm, from Old Swedish alboghi, from Old Norse ǫlnbogi, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô. Cognate with English elbow.
From earlier Swedish aderton, from Old Swedish atertan, from Old Norse átján, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun.

parole.significato: inheritance; the passing of titles, property etc upon someone's death
parole.testo: From Old Norse arfr (“heritage”), from Proto-Germanic *arbiją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“to change ownership”).
From Old Swedish arvoþe (“work; chore”), from Old Norse erfiði (“toil; hard work”), from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiją (“toil; work; hardship”). Doublet of arbete.
From Old Swedish asker, from Old Norse askr, from Proto-Germanic *askaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ōs- (“ash”).
From Old Norse aska, from Proto-Germanic *askǭ, probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs-.

parole.significato: Aspen; a type of poplar tree. (Populus tremula)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ǫsp, from Proto-Germanic *aspō, from Proto-Indo-European *Hosp- (“aspen, poplar”).
Borrowed from Old Norse ást, from Proto-Germanic *anstiz.
From Old Norse af, from Proto-Germanic *ab.

Equivalent to av- + rätta. Originally from Old Swedish rætta (“execute”), from Old Norse rétta, from Proto-Germanic *rihtijaną. Prefixed by analogy to Middle Low German africhten. Compare Danish afrette, Norwegian avretta, German abrichten.
From Old Swedish afund, from Old Norse ǫfund, from Proto-Germanic *abundiz.
From Old Swedish axl, from Old Norse ǫxl, from Proto-Germanic *ahslō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs-.

parole.significato: a hill (portion of a road or other path sloping lengthwise – compare kulle (“hill (elevated landmass)”))
parole.testo: From Old Norse bakki (“bank”), from Proto-Germanic *bankô.

parole.significato: bathing; swimming (see the usage notes for bada, which also apply here)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish badh, from Old Norse bað, from Proto-Germanic *baþą, from the zero-grade of Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₁-.

parole.significato: to bathe (immerse oneself or someone else in water (or another liquid), for cleaning, recreation, etc. – see the usage…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish badha, from Old Norse baða, from Proto-Germanic *baþōną.
From Old Swedish bakare, bagare, baghare, from Old Norse bakari, from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz. Akin to baka + -are.
From Old Swedish baker, from Old Norse bak, from Proto-Germanic *baką. Related to English back.

parole.significato: back-, at the back, behind, emphasis on 1st syllable
parole.testo: From Old Swedish baker, from Old Norse bak, from Proto-Germanic *baką. Related to English back.

parole.significato: to bake; to cook in an oven.
parole.testo: From Old Norse baka, from Proto-Germanic *bakaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₃g-.
From bak- (“back-”) + tala (“talk”), ultimately from Old Norse tala, from Proto-Germanic *talō (“calculation, number”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“to reckon, count”).
From Old Swedish balker, from Old Norse bialki, bǫlkr, from Proto-Germanic *balkuz, from *balkô (“beam, plank”).

From Old Swedish balder, baller, from Old Norse bǫllr, from Proto-Germanic *balluz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blow, inflate, swell”). Doublet of boll and bulle. Compare Old English bealluc, English bollock, Danish balde (“buttock”). First attested in 1520.

As a simplex noun a borrowing from Old Swedish bani, from Old Norse bani, from Proto-Germanic *banô, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰon-on-, from the o-grade of *gʷʰen- (“to strike, to kill”). Cognate to English bane, Icelandic bani. The word can be regarded as a reborrowing from Old Swedish mediaeval

parole.significato: to repeatedly strike something with a fist or hard object
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bånga, from Old Norse banga, from Proto-Germanic *bang- (“to beat, pound”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰen- (“to beat, injure”).
From Old Norse banna, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną.

parole.significato: bare, uncovered; not covered by e.g. clothes (about people), fur (about certain animals) or a snow cover (about the gro…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bar, from Old Norse *barr (Old West Norse berr), from Proto-Germanic *bazaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰosós.
From Old Swedish bara, from Old Norse *bara (“barely, only”), from *barr, from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (“bare”). Compare Icelandic bara.

parole.significato: bark (covering of the trunk of a tree)
parole.testo: From Old Norse bǫrkr, from Proto-Germanic *barkuz.
Inherited from Old Swedish barmber, from Old Norse barmr, from Proto-Germanic *barmaz. Cognate with Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐍂𐌼𐍃 (barms), Icelandic barmur, Old English bearm.

parole.significato: a child (person who has not reached adulthood)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish barn (“child”), from Old Norse barn (“child”), from Proto-Germanic *barną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-. Cognate with Danish barn, Icelandic barn, Old Saxon barn, Old High German barn, Latvian bērns (“child”), Lithuanian bérnas (“worker”) and bernẽlis (“lad”), a kind of participl

parole.significato: to ask for, request someone else to do something
parole.testo: From older bedja, from Old Swedish biþia, from Old Norse biðja, from Proto-Germanic *bidjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰedʰ-. Cognate with Danish bede, Icelandic biðja, English bid, Dutch bidden, German bitten.
From Old Swedish bēn, from Old Norse bein, from Proto-Germanic *bainą.
From Old Norse bjarg, berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ-.
From Old Swedish bī, bȳ, from Old Norse bý, from Proto-Germanic *bijō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰī-.
From Old Swedish bīþa, from Old Norse bíða, from Proto-Germanic *bīdaną.

parole.significato: a share; the cutting blade of a plough
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bilder, from Old Norse bíldr, from Proto-Germanic *bīþlaz (“axe”). An instrumental derivation of *bītaną (“to bite”). Closely related to bila (“broadaxe”).

parole.significato: to tie (fasten with ropes or strings)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish binda, from Old Norse binda, from Proto-Germanic *bindaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ-.
From Old Norse bíta, from Proto-Germanic *bītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).

parole.significato: to offer, to give as a gift
parole.testo: From Old Swedish biūþa, from Old Norse bjóða, from Proto-Germanic *beudaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to wake, rise up”).
From Old Norse bjalki, from Proto-Germanic *balkô, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ-.
Variant of bjälla, possibly blended with skallra. From Old Swedish biælla, from Old Norse bjalla, from Proto-Germanic *bellǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-.
From Old Norse bjǫrk, from Proto-Germanic *berkō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵós.
From Old Swedish biorn, biørn, from Old Norse bjǫrn, from Proto-Germanic *bernuz, northern form of Proto-Germanic *berô, probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“brown”).

parole.significato: a leaf (including in the broad sense that includes needles and the like (to botanists and often not to other people, in…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish blaþ, from Old Norse blað, from Proto-Germanic *bladą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₃-tó-m, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃-. Cognate with English blade.
From Old Norse blanda, from Proto-Germanic *blandaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-.

From Old Norse bleikr, from Proto-Germanic *blaikaz. Cognate with English bleak, Dutch bleek, Low German blek, German bleich, Danish bleg, Norwegian Bokmål bleik, blek, Norwegian Nynorsk bleik, Faroese bleikur, Icelandic bleikur.

parole.significato: to bleach; to make whiter or paler
parole.testo: From Old Swedish blēkia, from Old Norse bleikja, from Proto-Germanic *blaikijaną, from *blaikaz, whence also blek.
From Old Norse blíkja, from Proto-Germanic *bliką (“look”), *blīkaną (“to shine, gleam”).

parole.significato: mild, kind (when describing a person's temperament)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bliþer, from Old Norse blíðr, from Proto-Germanic *blīþiz (“mild; kind”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“shine”). Cognate of Icelandic blíður, English blithe, and Dutch blij.

parole.significato: blind; unable or failing to see
parole.testo: From Old Swedish blinder, from Old Norse blindr, from Proto-Germanic *blindaz.
From Old Swedish blōþ, from Old Norse blóð, from Proto-Germanic *blōþą (“blood”).
From Old Swedish blōme, from Old Norse blómi, blóm, from Proto-Germanic *blōmô.

parole.significato: drag, puff (on a cigarette, cigar, or pipe)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish blos, blus, from Old Norse blys, from Proto-Germanic *blusją (“firebrand, torch”). Related to Swedish bläs (“blaze”).
From Old Swedish blot, from Old Norse blót, from Proto-Germanic *blōtą.
From Old Swedish blota, from Old Norse blóta, from Proto-Germanic *blōtaną. Compare Danish blote, Old English blotan.

parole.significato: a blaze, especially on a horse
parole.testo: From Old Norse blesi, from Proto-Germanic *blasį̄, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shine”).
From Old Norse blár (“blue”), from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue”).
From Old Norse blása (“to blow”), from Proto-Germanic *blēsaną. Cognate with Elfdalian blåsa, Norwegian Nynorsk blåsa and Danish blæse
From Old Swedish blāster, blǣster‚ from Old Norse blástr, from Proto-Germanic *blēstuz.
From Old Swedish blø̄þa, from Old Norse blǿða, from Proto-Germanic *blōdijaną.

parole.significato: wet (covered with or impregnated with liquid)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish blø̄ter, from Old Norse blautr (“wet”), bleyta, from Proto-Germanic *blautaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlaw-.

parole.significato: to live, to dwell, to reside (to have permanent residence)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bō, bōa, from Old Norse búa, from Proto-Germanic *būaną.

parole.significato: a buck; the male of goat and deer
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bukker, bokker, from Old Norse bokkr, bukkr, from Proto-Germanic *bukkaz‚ from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuǵ-nó-.
From Old Swedish boþ, from Old Norse bóð (Compare Old West Norse búð), from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (“dwelling”).
Inherited from Old Swedish bōgher, from Old Norse bógr, from Proto-Germanic *bōguz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰāǵʰus.
From Old Swedish bōk, from Old Norse bók, from Proto-Germanic *bōks, of uncertain origin but usually connected to Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵ- (“beech”) or Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂g- (“to allot”).
From Old Swedish bōk, from Old Norse bók, from Proto-Germanic *bōkō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos.
From Old Swedish bōkstaver, from Old Norse bókstafr, from Proto-Germanic *bōkastabaz. Compare English bookstaff.

parole.significato: a ball; a more or less spherical object which is not hard or unyielding (compare kula)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish balder, baller, from Old Norse bǫllr (“ball, globe”), from Proto-Germanic *balluz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoln- (“round thing, bubble”), from *bʰel- (“to blow, inflate, swell”).

parole.significato: a bolster (a large cushion or pillow)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bulster, bolster, from Old Norse bólstr, bulstr, from Proto-Germanic *bulstraz m, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“bag, pillow, paunch”).
From Old Swedish borþ, from Old Norse borð, from Proto-Germanic *burdą.

From Old Swedish borin, burin, from Old Norse borinn, from Proto-Germanic *buranaz, from Proto-Germanic *beraną, the root of bära (“to carry, bear, lead up to”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-. Cognate with English born, and a doublet of buren.

From Old Swedish borgh (“fortress, city”), from Old Norse borg (also "bulwark", "wall'), from Proto-Germanic *burgz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ-. Akin to English borough, burgh, Old Irish bri (hence the name Birgitta).

parole.significato: to act as a guarantee for (that), to greatly increase the likelihood (that)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish borgha, from Old Norse borga, from Proto-Germanic *burgōną.

parole.significato: to drill, to bore (make a hole with a drill or other boring instrument, through twisting and pressure)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bora, from Old Norse bora, from Proto-Germanic *burōną. Equivalent to borr + -a.
From Old Swedish borst, from Old Norse burst, from Proto-Germanic *burstiz (“bristle”).

From Old Swedish bōt (“improvement”), from Old Norse ᛒᚢᛏ (but) (in the Latin script bót) whence also Icelandic bót), from Proto-Germanic *bōtō. Akin to English boot (“remedy, profit”). Masculine in Late Modern Swedish.

parole.significato: bottom (lowest part; lowest part of a container; bed of a body of water)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish butn, botn, from Old Norse botn, from Proto-Germanic *butmaz.

From Old Swedish bragþ (“rapid move; invention, artifice”), from Old Norse bragð (“action”). Compare Norwegian bragd f (“manner, appearance, action”), bragd n (“light, glimt”) (compare Swedish bragda (“to shine, to twinkle”)), Old Norse bragð (“moment, action, trick, appearance, change, figure on cl

parole.significato: a larger, uncontrolled fire (due to an accident, arson, or the like), a conflagration
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brander, from Old Norse brandr, from Proto-Germanic *brandaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenu-. A derivative of brinna.
From Old Swedish brēþer, from Old Norse breiðr, from Proto-Germanic *braidaz.
From Old Swedish brēþa, from Old Norse breiða, from Proto-Germanic *braidijaną.
From Old Swedish bred, from Old Norse breidd, from Proto-Germanic *braidiþō, equivalent to bred + -d.
From Old Swedish brista, from Old Norse bresta, from Proto-Germanic *brestaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰres- (“to burst, break, crack, split, separate”).

parole.significato: a brother (this is the original form more commonly contracted to bror)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brōþir, from Old Norse bróðir, from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.

parole.significato: a brother, a contracted form of broder
parole.testo: From Old Swedish broþir, from Old Norse bróðir (“brother”), from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr. Compare English bro.

From Old Swedish brusk, from Old Norse brjósk (“gristle, cartilage”), from Proto-Germanic *breuską, *breutską, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to swell, break forth, sprout”). Cognate with Danish brusk, Icelandic brjósk.

parole.significato: a break, a snap; an instance of something breaking
parole.testo: From Old Norse brot, from Proto-Germanic *brutą, derived from the verb *breutaną (cf. Swedish bryta).
From Old Swedish brūþ, from Old Norse brúðr (“bride”), from Proto-Germanic *brūdiz.

parole.significato: groom, bridegroom (a man on his wedding day, just before it or a short time after it)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brūþgumi, from Old Norse brúðgumi, from Proto-Germanic *brūdigumô. Compare Danish and Norwegian brudgom, Icelandic brúðgumi, Faroese brúðgómur.

parole.significato: a well (hole sunk into the ground, as a source for drinking water or a drain for waste water)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brunder, from Old Norse brunnr, bruðr, from Proto-Germanic *brunna-.

parole.significato: a relatively small pier (supported on piles or cribs, or floating on pontoons) used for mooring small boats or for bath…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bryggia, from Old Norse bryggja, from Proto-Germanic *brugjǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerw-, *bʰrēw-.

parole.significato: to brew (to prepare liquor or coffee)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bryggia, from Old Norse *bryggja, from Proto-Germanic *brewwaną.
From Old Norse brún, from Proto-Germanic *brūwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃bʰrúHs.
From Old Swedish brȳta, from Old Norse brjóta, from Proto-Germanic *breutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewd-.

parole.significato: A fern, especially the bracken fern Pteris aquilina.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brækne, from Old Norse *brakni (“undergrowth”), related to Proto-Germanic *brekaną and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”). Compare Danish bregne, English bracken.

parole.significato: to burn (something – see the usage notes below)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brænna, from Old Norse brenna, from Proto-Germanic *brannijaną.

parole.significato: sudden, hasty, busy, full of hurry
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brāþer, from Old Norse bráðr (“hasty, sudden”), from Proto-Germanic *brēþaz (“hot, in a hurry, rushed”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrē-, *bʰerē- (“steam, vapour”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to seethe, toss about, cook”). Cognate with Icelandic bráður.
From Old Swedish brø̄þ, from Old Norse brauð, from Proto-Germanic *braudą. Cognate with Dutch brood, German Brot, English bread, Danish brød, Icelandic brauð.
From Old Swedish būker, from Old Norse búkr, from Proto-Germanic *būkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōw-. Doublet of buga, böja, and bukt.

parole.significato: unpleasant noise (usually associated with mechanical sources such as engines and machinery rather than electric/electro…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bulder. Arguably from Old Norse, from or related to Proto-Germanic *bellaną (“to roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-. Deverbal from bullra.
From Old Swedish būr, from Old Norse búr, from Proto-Germanic *būrą.

parole.significato: a bush; a shrub (category of plants distinguished from trees by having multiple stems and lower height)
parole.testo: From Old Norse buskr (compare Danish and Norwegian busk, Icelandic búskur), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (compare English bush, Dutch bos, German Busch).

From Old Swedish bȳr, bȳ (“village, farm, town”), from Old Norse býr. Cognate with Danish by (“town, city”, whence also Faroese býur with the same meaning), Norwegian Bokmål by (“town, city”) and Norwegian Nynorsk by (“town, city”).

parole.significato: An (often vaguely defined) rural region (forming a cohesive community in some sense; e.g. historical, cultural, or geog…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish byghþ, from Old Norse byggð, from Proto-Germanic *biwwiþō. First attested in the 13th century. Doublet of bygga (“build”).
From Old Swedish bækker, from Old Norse bekkr, from Proto-Germanic *bakiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰog-. Compare English beck

parole.significato: a (simple) bed; a place arranged where to sleep
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bädh, from Old Norse beðr, from Proto-Germanic *badją.

From Old Swedish bælgher, from Old Norse belgr, from Proto-Germanic *balgiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”). Cognate of Danish bælg, Dutch balg, German Balg, Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌻𐌲𐍃 (balgs). Doublet of bölja (“wave”), cognate to English bulge. Related to Swedish boll (“ball”), bulle (“bun”), bu

From Old Swedish bælghia (“to swell up”), from Old Norse belgja (“to inflate”), from Proto-Germanic *balgijaną, causative of *belganą. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”). Compare Danish bælle.

parole.significato: a belt (around the waist, or around the torso or the like, of for example a seat belt (säkerhetsbälte) – compare rem)
parole.testo: From Old Norse belti, from Proto-Germanic *baltijaz (“belt”), from Latin balteus.

parole.significato: pry (open something by means of leverage)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish bænda, from Old Norse benda, from Proto-Germanic *bandijaną. Cognate of English bend.

parole.significato: bench, a long sofa without bolster
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bænker, from (East) Old Norse *benkr (cf. West Old Norse bekkr), from Proto-Germanic *bankiz.
From Old Swedish bær, from Old Norse ber, from Proto-Germanic *bazją.

parole.significato: to carry; to lift and transport anywhere else
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bæra, from Old Norse bera, from Proto-Germanic *beraną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (whence also börja, bår and barn). Cognate with Danish bære, Norwegian bære, and English bear.

parole.significato: to salvage (recover, most commonly (something on) a sunken vessel, or a vehicle that has broken down)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish biærgha, bærgha, from Old Norse bjarga, from Proto-Germanic *berganą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ-. Cognate of Icelandic bjarga, Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌲𐌰𐌽 (bairgan), German bergen, Old English beorgan.
From Old Swedish bæria, from Old Norse berja, from Proto-Germanic *barjaną.
From Old Norse bifa, from Proto-Germanic *bibāną (“to quake, shiver”).
From Old Swedish buþa, bodha, from Old Norse boða, Proto-Germanic *budōną.
From Old Swedish bāþe, from Old Norse báðir (“both”), from Proto-Germanic *bai, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰóh₁. Cognate with English both.
From Old Swedish bughi, from Old Norse bogi, from Proto-Germanic *bugô.
From Old Norse bál (“fire”), from Proto-Germanic *bēlą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“light, bright”).

parole.significato: a barrow, a litter (tool for carrying)
parole.testo: From Old Norse bára, from Proto-Germanic *bērō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.

parole.significato: a booth, a stall, (at a stadium) a box
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bas, from Old Norse báss, from Proto-Germanic *bansaz. More at boose.
From Old Swedish bø̄ghia, from Old Norse beygja, from Proto-Germanic *baugijaną.

parole.significato: a wave, a billow (large, undulating wave, like on the sea)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bylghia, from Old Norse bylgja, from Proto-Germanic *bulgijō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ-.
From Old Swedish bø̄n, from Old Norse bǿn, bœn, bón (whence English boon), from Proto-Germanic *bōniz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to speak, to say”). Cognate with Danish bøn, Old English bēn.
From Old Swedish bøna, bøn, from Old Norse baun, from Proto-Germanic *baunō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ-, *bʰabʰ-eh₂-. The final -a was added under Middle Low German influence.
From the verb bära, just like English birth relates to the verb bear. From Old Swedish byrþ, from Old Norse burðr, byrð, Proto-Germanic *burdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.
From Old Norse *byrðr, burðr, from Proto-Germanic *burþį̄, related to bära (“to bear, to carry”) and börd (“birth”).
From Old Swedish byria, from Old Norse byrja, from Proto-Germanic *burjaną. Derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.

parole.significato: to pay a fine, to be fined
parole.testo: From Old Norse bǿta, from Proto-Germanic *bōtijaną.
Old Swedish blakker, from Old Norse blakkr, from Proto-Germanic *blankaz. Doublet of black and blank.

From Old Swedish dag, dagh, dagg, from Old Norse dagg (“dew”), from Proto-Germanic *dawwō (“dew, moisture”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze”). Cognate with Danish dug (“dew”). Doublet of dugg (“drizzle”).

From Old Swedish damb, dåm (“dust, steam”), from Old Norse dumba (“dust, cloud of dust”), from or related to Proto-Germanic *dampaz (“vapor”). Akin to Low German damp, Dutch damp, and Danish damp (“vapor, steam, fog”), German Dampf, Icelandic dampi, English damp (“moderately wet”), and to German dam
From Old Swedish damber, dampn, from Old Norse dammr, from Proto-Germanic *dammaz.
From Old Swedish dan, from Old Norse danir, from Proto-Germanic *daniz.

From Old Swedish darra, from Old Norse dirre (“to shake”), from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *dʰerh₃- (“to spring, leap”), see also Ancient Greek θρῴσκω (thrōískō). A probable Germanic cognate is Dutch dartel (“playful, frisky”).
From Old Norse darr, from Proto-Germanic *darōþuz.

parole.significato: the, a definite article used in the beginning of noun phrases containing attributive adjectives and nouns in the plural…
parole.testo: From Old Norse þeir, from Proto-Germanic *þai (with noun ending -r).

parole.significato: dough; a thick mix of flour and water
parole.testo: From Old Swedish dēgher, from Old Norse deig, from Proto-Germanic *daigaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead, to mold, to form”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål deig, Norwegian Nynorsk deig, Icelandic deig, Faroese deiggj, Danish dej.

parole.significato: to deal, share; divide something between recipients
parole.testo: From Old Swedish dēla, from Old Norse deila, from Proto-Germanic *dailijaną.
From Old Swedish þæn, accusative of sā(r), from Old Norse sá, from Proto-Germanic *sa, from Proto-Indo-European *só.

From Old Swedish þēra, from Old Norse þeirra, with the -s added in analogy with other genitive forms, specifically the masculine/neuter singular -s. Further from Proto-Germanic *þaizǫ̂, genitive plural of *sa, and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tóysoHom, masculine/neuter genitive plural of Pro

parole.significato: it; third-person singular, referring to nouns of neuter gender. Nominative, accusative or dative
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þæt, dhet‚ from Old Norse þat, from Proto-Germanic *þat, from Proto-Indo-European *tod, nominative and accusative singular neuter of *só.
From Old Norse þik, from Proto-Germanic *þek, from Proto-Indo-European *te-ge.
From Old Swedish digher, from Old Norse digr, from Proto-Germanic *digraz.

parole.significato: ditch; a small canal, for irrigation or drainage
parole.testo: From Old Norse díki, from Proto-Germanic *dīkiją, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ-. Cognate with English dike, ditch.
From Old Swedish dil, from Old Norse dylja, from Proto-Germanic *dilja-, of uncertain, non-Indo-European origin, possibly a substrate.
From Old Swedish þīn, from Old Norse þínn, from Proto-Germanic *þīnaz.

parole.significato: deep (having a certain or great depth, sometimes more abstractly)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish diūper, from Old Norse djúpr, from Proto-Germanic *deupaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb-.

parole.significato: depth (how deep something is, in the senses above)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish diūp, from Old Norse djúp, from a nominalization of Proto-Germanic *deupaz (see above).

From Old Swedish diærver, from Old Norse djarfr, from Proto-Germanic *derbaz. According to Svenska Akademiens ordbok it may be related to the same stem as Old English deorfan ("to work; to act") and Lithuanian dirbti ("to work"), or Ancient Greek τρέφω (tréphō) ("to make solid; to make fat; to feed;
From Old Norse dokka, from Proto-Germanic *dokko (“something round”), related to *dukkǭ (“muscle, strength”).

parole.significato: conviction, judgement of court, sentence, verdict, doom
parole.testo: From Old Norse dómr (“judgement”), from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰóh₁mos.

parole.significato: to pull (on something, possibly causing it to move)
parole.testo: Apocopic form of draga, from Old Swedish dragha, from Old Norse draga, from Proto-Germanic *draganą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreǵ-. In some senses, from Middle Low German dragen (“carry”) (compare German tragen).
Inherited from Old Swedish draf, from Old Norse draf, from Proto-Germanic *drabaz.

parole.significato: a drive (of hunters), a beat, a battue
parole.testo: From Old Norse dreif, from Proto-Germanic *draibō, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ-.
From Old Swedish drikka, from Old Norse drekka, from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną. The noun is derived from the verb.
From Old Norse dript, from Proto-Germanic *driftiz.

From Old Swedish drīva, from Old Norse drífa, from Proto-Germanic *drībaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”). Compare Danish and Norwegian drive, Icelandic drífa, English drive, Frisian driuwe, Dutch drijven, German treiben.
From Old Swedish drupi, dropi, from Old Norse dropi, from Proto-Germanic *drupô, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrew- (“to crumble, grind”).
From Old Swedish drotin (with -in interpreted as the definite suffix), from Old Norse dróttinn, from Proto-Germanic *druhtinaz. Related to dryg (lasting, heavy).
From Old Swedish drykker, from Old Norse drykkr, from Proto-Germanic *drunkiz.
From Old Swedish drȳgher, from Old Norse drjúgr, from Proto-Germanic *dreugaz. Cognate to Russian друг (drug, “friend”).
From Old Norse dregg (“sediment”), from Proto-Germanic *dragjō (whence also Icelandic dregg, English dreg).
From Old Swedish drænger (“young man, boy, servant”), from Old Norse drengr (“boy; log, pole”), from Proto-Germanic *drangijaz. See also Danish dreng (“boy”).

parole.significato: cause to drown; to deprive of life by immersion in water or other liquid.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish drænkia, from Old Norse drekkja, drenkja, from Proto-Germanic *drankijaną, causative of *drinkaną.
From Old Swedish dræpa, Old Norse drepa (“to hit; to kill”), from Proto-Germanic *drepaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dhrebh-. Doublet of drabba and träffa.
Inherited from Old Swedish *drøgher, Old Norse draugr, Proto-Germanic *draugaz (“delusion, mirage, illusion”).

parole.significato: a dream (imaginary events seen in the mind while sleeping)
parole.testo: From Old Norse draumr, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz. Cognate to English dream.

parole.significato: to dream; to see imaginary events in one's mind while sleeping
parole.testo: From Old Swedish drø̄ma, from Old Norse dreyma, from Proto-Germanic *draumijaną. Cognate to English dream, Dutch dromen and German träumen.

parole.significato: drone; a male of social aculeatas which includes mosquito, bee, wasp, and ant
parole.testo: From Old Norse *drán, from Proto-Germanic *drēnuz.
From Old Swedish þū, from Old Norse þú, from Proto-Germanic *þū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognate with English thou, German du.

parole.significato: to be good enough; to suffice, to be acceptable, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish dugha, from Old Norse duga, from Proto-Germanic *duganą. The (formerly) colloquial strong declension mirrors the declensions of words like suga and ljuga.

parole.significato: tablecloth; a similar piece of cloth used for protection or decoration of e.g. a chest of drawers
parole.testo: From Old Norse dúkr, from Proto-Germanic *dōkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dwōg-, *dwōk-.

From Old Swedish dumber, from Old Norse dumbr, from Proto-Germanic *dumbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-. Compare Norwegian dumb, Danish dum, Icelandic dumbur, English dumb, Dutch dom and German dumm.
From Old Swedish dūva, from Old Norse dúfa, from Proto-Germanic *dūbǭ. Compare Danish and Norwegian Bokmål due, Icelandic dúfa, Dutch duif, German Taube, English dove.

parole.significato: dormancy, hibernation (non-pathological (or peaceful or the like) dormant, extended, restful, sleep-like state, sometim…
parole.testo: From Old Norse dvala, dvalan, from Proto-Germanic *dwalaz (“stunned, confused”). Related to Old Norse dvelja (“to remain, stay, to delay”).

parole.significato: dwarf (any member of a race of beings from Germanic folklore)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish dværgher, from Old Norse dvergr, from Proto-Germanic *dwergaz.

From Old Swedish dyghþ (“virtue”), from Old Norse dygð, cognate with Norwegian dygd, Danish dyd, from Proto-Germanic *dugiþō, a variant of *dugunþō in English douth, German Tugend, Dutch deugd. These words are derived from the verb *duganą (“to be useful”), hence Swedish duga.

From Old Swedish dygn, dyghn, døgn, døghn, from Old Norse dœgn, from Proto-Germanic *dōgin-, alternative form of *dōg-. First attested in the mid-14th century. Cognate with Danish døgn, Norwegian Bokmål døgn and Norwegian Nynorsk døgn. See also Old Norse dœgr, Norwegian Nynorsk døger and Icelandic d

parole.significato: a cushion (for use as a seat or backrest, for lying on, or the like – most commonly rectangular – compare kudde)
parole.testo: From Old Norse dýna, from Proto-Germanic *dūnaz (“fluffy feathers”).
From Old Swedish dyngia, from Old Norse dyngja, from Proto-Germanic *dungijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ-.
From Old Swedish dȳr, from Old Norse dýrr, from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz. Cognate with English dear.
Inherited from Old Swedish dængia, from Old Norse dengja, from Proto-Germanic *dangijaną. Doublet of dingla.
From Old Norse þar, from Proto-Germanic *þar.
From Old Swedish þā, from Old Norse þá, from Proto-Germanic *þan (“then”).
From Old Swedish dāþ, from Old Norse dáð, from Proto-Germanic *dēdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁tis, from *dʰeh₁- (“to place, set, put”). Cognate with Old English dǣd (whence English deed).

parole.significato: din, rumble, roar; a low, loud sound
parole.testo: From Old Swedish dyn, from Old Norse dynr, from Proto-Germanic *duniz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwen-. Cognate with English din. Doublet of dön.

From Old Swedish dø̄ia, from Old Norse deyja (“to die”) (compare English die), from Proto-Germanic *dawjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew-. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål dø, Danish dø, Icelandic deyja.
From Old Swedish dø̄þer, from Old Norse dauðr (“dead”), from Proto-Germanic *daudaz.
From Old Swedish dø̄þer, from Old Norse dauðr (“death”), from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz.
From Old Norse deyða, from Proto-Germanic *daudijaną.
From Old Swedish dø̄ma, from Old Norse dǿma, from Proto-Germanic *dōmijaną.

parole.significato: to baptize, to christen (perform the religious act of baptism upon)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish dø̄pa, from Old Norse deypa, from Proto-Germanic *daupijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb-.
From Old Swedish dyr, from Old Norse dyrr, from Proto-Germanic *durz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door, gate”).
Inherited from Old Swedish dys, from Old Norse dys (“grave mound”), from an earlier Proto-Germanic *dusjō-.
From Old Swedish dø̄ver, from Old Norse daufr, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, be obscured”).
From Old Norse æ, ei, ey, from Proto-Germanic *aiwi (“forever”), *aiwaz.

parole.significato: prefix that may be used on certain pronouns and adverbs to create "-ever" constructions, most of which are formal or ar…
parole.testo: From Old Norse æ, from Proto-Germanic *aiwi (“forever”), Proto-Germanic *aiwaz.
From Old Swedish ēþer, from Old Norse eiðr, from Proto-Germanic *aiþaz.

parole.significato: An isthmus; a strip of land between two bodies of water
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ēþ, from Old Norse eið, from Proto-Germanic *aidiją, probably related to Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey- (“go”) and Latin eo. Cognate with Norwegian eid, Icelandic eið, and Faroese eið.
From earlier edar, from Old Swedish iþar, idhar, from Old Norse *iðwarr (possessive of *īʀ, East Norse form of ér), from Proto-Germanic *izweraz.

parole.significato: peculiar, eccentric, odd, unique, personal, individualistic
parole.testo: From Old Norse eiginn, from Proto-Germanic *aiganaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *aiganą. Equivalent to äga + -en. Cognate with English own.

parole.significato: The sharp edge of a cutting tool.
parole.testo: From Old Norse egg, from Proto-Germanic *agjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”).
From Old Norse eik, from Proto-Germanic *aiks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“oak”).
From Old Swedish ikorne, ekorne, from Old Norse íkorni, from Proto-Germanic *aikwernô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer-.

parole.significato: fire (continued chemical exothermic reaction where a gaseous material reacts, and which creates enough heat to evaporat…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish elder, from Old Norse eldr, from Proto-Germanic *ailidaz.
From Old Swedish ælla, ællar, from Old Norse ella, ellar, from Proto-Germanic *aljaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos.

parole.significato: object form of the indefinite pronoun man ("one," "you")
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ēn, æn, from Old Norse einn, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one, some”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one”).

parole.significato: Lacking knowledge and wits; stupid, simple, fatuous.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish enfaldogher (“folded once”) (older form enfalder), from en (“one”) + fåll (“crease; fold”) + -ig (“-y”), from Old Norse einfaldr, from Proto-Germanic *ainafalþaz. Related to English onefold. Akin to en + -faldig.

parole.significato: agreeing, in agreement (sharing the same opinion)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish enigh, from Old Norse einigr, from Proto-Germanic *ainagaz (“singular, sole, only”).

parole.significato: your, yours (possessed by the multiple individuals addressed, of multiple things)
parole.testo: From Old Norse yðr, yðar, from Proto-Germanic *izwiz.

parole.significato: atter, such as venom, poison (from an animal or plant)
parole.testo: From Old Norse eitr, from Proto-Germanic *aitrą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyd-.
From Old Swedish faþir, from Old Norse faðir, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.
From Old Swedish fagher, from Old Norse fagr, from Proto-Germanic *fagraz, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂ḱ- (“to fasten, place”).
From Old Swedish falla, from Old Norse falla, from Proto-Germanic *fallaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂p-h₃elh₁-.
From Old Swedish fana, from Old Norse fani, from Proto-Germanic *fanô, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂n-.
Short for fader, from Old Norse faðir, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr (“father”).
From Old Swedish fara, from Old Norse fara, from Proto-Germanic *faraną, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“going, passage”).
From Old Swedish faster, from Old Norse fastr, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz; see it for cognates and further etymology.
From Old Swedish fasta, from Old Norse fasta, from Proto-Germanic *fastāną.
From Old Norse fat, from Proto-Germanic *fatą, from Proto-Indo-European *pod-.
From Old Swedish fēgher, from Old Norse feigr, from Proto-Germanic *faigijaz. The present meaning ("cowardly") is through German influence (compare German feige).
PIE word  *pénkʷe From Old Norse fimm (“five”), from Proto-Germanic *fimf, ultimately from *pémpe, variant of Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe.
From Old Swedish fæmte, fæmpte, femte, fæmti, from Old Norse fimti, from Proto-Germanic *fimftô.
From Old Swedish fæmtan, from Old Norse fimmtán, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun.
From Old Swedish fēter, from Old Norse feitr, from Proto-Germanic *faitaz.

parole.significato: an enemy (person, etc., opposed to oneself)
parole.testo: From Old Norse fjándi, from Proto-Germanic *fijandz, corresponding to the present participle of the verb fjá (“hate”). Compare Danish fjende, Icelandic fjandi, German Feind, English fiend.
From Old Swedish finger, from Old Norse fingr, from Proto-Germanic *fingraz, from Proto-Indo-European *penkʷrós.

parole.significato: to find, to locate, to discover
parole.testo: From Old Swedish finna, from Old Norse finna, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass; path, bridge”).

parole.significato: to fart (emit flatulent gases through the anus)
parole.testo: From Old Norse físa (“to break wind”), from Proto-Germanic *fīsaną (“to break wind”).
From Old Swedish fisker, from Old Norse fiskr, from Proto-Germanic *fiskaz (“fish”), from Proto-Indo-European *peysk- (“fish”).
From Old Norse fiska, from Proto-Germanic *fiskōną. Corresponds to fisk + -a.
From Old Norse fiskari, from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz, equivalent of fiska (“fish”) + -are (“-er”). Cognate with Norwegian fisker, Danish fisker.

parole.significato: used adverbially in the prepositional phrase i fjor (“last year”) – yesteryear, last year
parole.testo: From Old Norse fjǫrð (in prepositional phrase í fjǫrð), from Proto-Germanic *ferudi (“last year”), from Proto-Indo-European *peruti (“last year”, literally “on the other side of a year”). Cognates include Ancient Greek πέρυσι (pérusi), Sanskrit परुत् (parut), and Old Irish uraid. Compare also Swedis
From Old Swedish fiughurtan, fiughertān, from Old Norse fjórtán, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun.

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish fiærdher, from Old Norse fjǫrðr (“firth, fjord”), from Proto-Germanic *ferþuz (“inlet, fjord”), from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”). Doublet of fjord.
From Old Swedish fiarþi, fiærþi, from Old Norse fjórði, from Proto-Germanic *fedurþô.

From Old Swedish fiætur, from Old Norse fjǫturr, from Proto-Germanic *feturaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“foot, step”).

parole.significato: a flock (group of animals (or people, by extension, often emphasizing lack of independence or the like))

From Old Norse flóð, from Proto-Germanic *flōduz, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₃tus. Compare Danish flod, Icelandic flóð, English flood, Dutch vloed, German Flut.

From Old Swedish flundra, from Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ (“flatfish”).

parole.significato: to flee, to run away, to escape

parole.significato: to fly (with wings, on an airplane, through the air, etc. – generally, like in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish flȳgha, from Old Norse fljúga, from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *plewk-.

parole.significato: to float; of an object or substance, to be supported by a fluid of greater density

From Old Swedish flytia, from Old Norse flytja, from Proto-Germanic *flutjaną.

Inherited from Old Swedish flætta, from Old Norse flétta, from Proto-Germanic *flehtaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ-.

parole.significato: to skin, to flay (remove the skin of an animal)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fla, from Old Norse flá, from Proto-Germanic *flahaną. Cognate with English flay.

parole.significato: to flow in great quantities (sometimes figuratively)

parole.significato: feed, fodder (food given to domestic animals)

From Old Norse *fukka, from Proto-Germanic *fukkōną.

From Old Norse fram, from Proto-Germanic *fram.
From Old Norse friðr, from Proto-Germanic *friþuz (cf. German Low German: Freed, Freden, as another possible influence).

From Old Norse freista, from Proto-Germanic *fraistōną.

From Old Swedish fræmia, fræmmia, from Old Norse fremja, from Proto-Germanic *framjaną, from Proto-Germanic *framaz.

From Old Swedish færia, from Old Norse ferja, from Proto-Germanic *farjǭ.

From Old Swedish galle, from Old Norse gall, from Proto-Germanic *gallǭ.

From Old Swedish gloa (“to glow”), from Old Norse glóa, from Proto-Germanic *glōaną.

From Old Swedish guþ, gudh, Old Norse guð, from Proto-Germanic *gudą.
From Old Norse gulr, from Proto-Germanic *gulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”).

From Old Swedish guldh (gwldh), gold, gol, gul, gull, from Old Norse gull, *gulð, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”). Compare Runic Old East Norse: ᚴᚢᛚ (kul /⁠ḡull⁠/), ᛁᚢᛚ (iul /⁠jull⁠/).

From gull, gul, gol, from Old Norse gull (compare Runic Old East Norse: ᚴᚢᛚ (kul /⁠ḡull⁠/), ᛁᚢᛚ (iul /⁠jull⁠/)), from Proto-Germanic *gulþą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”). Compare alternative form Old Swedish gold, guldh, gwldh, Old Norse *gulð. Cognate to Swedish gu
Learned borrowing from Old Norse gyðja, from Proto-Germanic *gudjǭ, feminine form of masculine *gudjô, the ancestor of goði.

parole.significato: golden, gold (made of gold (or covered in gold leaf or gold paint or the like))
parole.testo: From the weak form of Old Norse *gullinn, from Proto-Germanic *gulþīnaz.

parole.significato: a gill (breathing organ of aquatic animals)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gjǫlnar f pl, from Proto-Germanic *gelunō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel-, distantly related to Ancient Greek χεῖλος (kheîlos, “snout, beak, lip”). Cognate with English gill, Danish gælle and Norwegian gjelle.
From Old Swedish giæld, from Old Norse gjald, from Proto-Germanic *geldą (“reward, gift, money”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”).
From Old Swedish giælda, giælla, gælla, from Old Norse gjalda, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”). Under influence from Middle Low German gelden, see gälla.

Used in Swedish since 1674, same as Icelandic gjallur, like Middle Low German adverb gelle (“loud”), based on the obsolete Swedish verb gälla (“to yell”), from Old Swedish gælla (from Old Norse gjalla, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną), cognate with Icelandic gjalla, Old High German gellan (German gelle

parole.significato: to be valid; to be correct or proper, to apply
parole.testo: From Old Swedish giælda, giælla, gælla, from Old Norse gjalda, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”). Under influence from Low German gelden, compare gälda. See also Icelandic gilda and Icelandic gildandi.
From earlier gälda, from Old Norse gelda (“to castrate”), from Proto-Germanic *galdijaną.
Inherited from Old Swedish gänger, from Old Norse gengr, from Proto-Germanic *gangiz. Compare Icelandic gengr, Norwegian Nynorsk gjeng and Danish gæng.

parole.significato: a deed, an action, a cost
parole.testo: From Old Swedish gærþ (“a deed, a cost, what must be done”), from Old Norse gørð, from Proto-Germanic *garwidō, related to the adjective *garwaz (“prepared, ready”). Related to göra (“to do”). Compare Icelandic gerð, Danish gærd.

parole.significato: gladly, happily, with keenness, (when synonymous with "gladly") willingly/readily
parole.testo: From Old Norse gjarna, from Proto-Germanic *gernô (“willingly, gladly”), the adverbial form of *gernaz (“willing”).
From Old Swedish gā, from Old Norse gá, from Proto-Germanic *gāną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁-. Akin to English go.
From Old Swedish ganger, from Old Norse gangr, from Proto-Germanic *gangaz.
From Old Swedish ganga, from Old Norse ganga, from Proto-Germanic *ganganą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ-.

parole.significato: a property with houses in the countryside (sometimes along with farmland, pasture, etc.); an estate, a homestead, a far…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish garþer, from Old Norse garðr, from Proto-Germanic *gardaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ- (“to enclose”).

From Old Swedish gās, from Old Norse gás, from Proto-Germanic *gans, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns (“goose”). Cognate with English goose, German Gans, etc. In the other senses referring to the goose’s ability to float on water.
Inherited from Old Swedish gava, from Old Norse gáfa, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gēbǭ.
From Old Swedish gø̄ker, from Old Norse gaukr, from Proto-Germanic *gaukaz.

parole.significato: place where things are hidden or stashed away
parole.testo: From Old Swedish gø̄ma, from Old Norse geyma, from Proto-Germanic *gaumijaną.

From an older noun gorr, går (“dirt, mud, animal intestine content etc.”), with western Swedish vowel fronting /ɔ/ > /œː/ (sometimes represented in dialectal writing with a circumflex ⟨ô⟩). * From Old Swedish gøra, gæra, giora, from Old Norse gera, gøra, gørva, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną. Compare with English yare and gear. * The noun is a nominalization of the verb. Literally "doing."

From an older noun gorr, går (“dirt, mud, animal intestine content etc.”), with western Swedish vowel fronting /ɔ/ > /œː/ (sometimes represented in dialectal writing with a circumflex ⟨ô⟩). From Old Swedish *giurdhil (attested in fægiurdhil), from older *gyrþil, from Old Norse gyrðill, from Proto-Germanic *gurdilaz, equivalent to gjorda (“to gird”) + -el (“instrumental suffix”). Influenced by Low German gördel.

parole.significato: a Geat person, a member of the Geats, a people allegedly having lived in Scandinavia, inhabitants of Götaland c
parole.testo: From Old Swedish gø̄tar, Old Norse gautar, from Proto-Germanic *gautaz. Further related to English Geat. The people mentioned as geatas in Beowulf, gautar in Icelandic sagas, gutones by Pliny, and gotones by Tacitus, have the problem that three different areas of Scandinavia have similar names: Jutl

parole.significato: To have; to possess, or to have as a property; to come into possession of something concrete or abstract.
parole.testo: Apocopic form of hava, from Old Swedish hava, from Old Norse hafa, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to take, seize, catch”).

parole.significato: an enclosed pasture; a pasture, a pen, a paddock
parole.testo: From Old Norse hagi, from Proto-Germanic *hagô, from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰom.

From Old Norse hagl, from Proto-Germanic *haglaz (“hail”), which may be from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰlos (“pebble, hail”). Cognates with Danish, Icelandic and Norwegian hagl, Old English hægl and hagol (English hail), Old Frisian heil, Old High German hagal (German Hagel) and Old Saxon hagal (Low G
From Old Swedish haghþorn, from Old Norse hagþorn, from Proto-Germanic *haguþurnuz, equivalent of hage (“enclosure, hedge”) + torn (“thorn”).

parole.significato: a hook (for fastening or suspending something, not fishing)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish haki, from Old Norse haki, from Proto-Germanic *hakô.
From Old Norse halmr, from Proto-Germanic *halmaz.

parole.significato: neck (of a person or animal) (compare nacke)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hals, from Proto-Germanic *halsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kólsos.

parole.significato: half, ½; with one of two equal parts (50 %)
parole.testo: From Old Norse halfr (“half”), from Proto-Germanic *halbaz.
From Old Swedish hamar, from Old Norse hamarr, from Proto-Germanic *hamaraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱmoros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éḱmō (“stone”).
From Old Swedish hamn, hampn, from Old Norse hǫfn, from Proto-Germanic *habnō.
From Old Swedish hampa, hamper, from Old Norse hampr, from Proto-Germanic *hanapiz.
From Old Swedish hand, from Old Norse hǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *handuz. Cognate with Danish hånd, Norwegian hand, German Hand, English hand.
From Old Swedish handla, from Old Norse handla, hǫndla, from Proto-Germanic *handlōną. In the sense trade influenced by from Middle Low German handelen and German handeln.
From Old Norse hani, from Proto-Germanic *hanô, from Proto-Indo-European *kan- (“to sing”).
From Old Swedish hari, hæri, from Old Norse *hari, heri, from Proto-Germanic *hesô.
From Old Swedish harpa, from Old Norse harpa, from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ. Compare Norwegian and Danish harpe, Icelandic harpa, Faroese hørpa, harpa, German Harfe, Dutch and English harp.
From Old Norse hatr, from Proto-Germanic *hataz.
From Old Swedish hata, from Old Norse hata, from Proto-Germanic *hatāną. By surface analysis, hat + -a.
From Old Swedish hatter, from Old Norse hǫttr, hattr, from Proto-Germanic *hattuz, from Proto-Indo-European *kadʰ- (“to guard, cover, care for, protect”).
From Old Swedish haf, from Old Norse haf, from Proto-Germanic *habą, and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-.
From Old Norse hafri, from Proto-Germanic *habrô, from Proto-Indo-European *kapro-.

parole.significato: A moor; an extensive waste land.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish heþ, from Old Norse heiðr, from Proto-Germanic *haiþī, from Proto-Indo-European *kayt-, *ḱayt-.
From Old Swedish heþin, from Old Norse heiðinn, from Proto-Germanic *haiþīnaz.

parole.significato: honour, dignity; what makes a person praiseworthy
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hēdher, from Old Norse heiðr, from Proto-Germanic *haiduz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kayt-, *(s)kaydʰ-.
From Old Norse heill, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz.
From Old Swedish hēla, from Old Norse heila, from Proto-Germanic *hailijaną. Equivalent to Swedish hel + -a.

parole.significato: to hallow, to keep holy, to sanctify
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hælgha, from Old Norse helga, from Proto-Germanic *hailagōną.
Inherited from Old Swedish hēlagher, hēligher, hælig, hælog, from Old Norse heilagr, from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz.

parole.significato: Hell (place where sinners go after death according to some religions)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hælffwætte, hælvīte, hælvīt, helvīte, from Old Norse helvíti, comprising of hel (“the death, underworld”) + vite (“penalty, punishment”), literally “penalty/punishment in death”, thought to stem from a Christian Pan-Germanic construction as Proto-Germanic *haljōwītiją, then likely a
From Old Norse heim < heimr, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz.

parole.significato: a whetstone, particularly the small and soft kind.
parole.testo: From Old Norse hein, from Proto-Germanic *hainō. Related to Norwegian and Icelandic hein (“whetstone”), Old English hān (“stone, rock”) and modern English hone. Further related to Sanskrit शाण (śāṇa) and Latin cōs with the same meaning. See also (dialectal) Swedish hena (“to hone”).
From Old Swedish hirþi, hirþe, herþe, herdhe, from Old Norse hirðir, from Proto-Germanic *hirdijaz. The ’boy’ sense developed because shepherds were typically young men.

parole.significato: hot; having a very high temperature
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hēter, from Old Norse heitr, from Proto-Germanic *haitaz.

parole.significato: to be called; to have as one's name, to hight
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hēta, from Old Norse heita, from Proto-Germanic *haitaną.
Partly from Old Swedish hita, partly from Old Swedish hēta, from Old Norse heita, from Proto-Germanic *haitijaną.

parole.significato: to prevent, restrain, hinder, impede, constrain
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hindra, from Old Norse hindra (“hinder, stay, delay”), probably from Proto-Germanic *hindrōną (“to put back”), from Proto-Indo-European *k(')enta (“down, below, with, far, along, against”), from *ḱen- (“to set oneself in motion, arise”).

parole.significato: to have time, to have the time (for something), (sometimes, idiomatically) to make it
parole.testo: From Old Norse *hinna (“to reach”), from Proto-Germanic *hinþaną.

parole.significato: a film, a skin (very thin (often elastic) layer, on for example milk, but general)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hinna, from Proto-Germanic *hinnǭ.
From Old Swedish hitta, from Old Norse hitta, from Proto-Germanic *hittijaną (“to come upon, find”), from Proto-Indo-European *keyd-.
Inherited from Old Swedish hion, from Old Norse hjón, hjún, hjú, from Proto-Germanic *hīwōnō.

parole.significato: herd; a number of beasts gathered
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hiorþ, from Old Norse hjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *herdō, from Proto-Indo-European *kerdʰ- (“file, row, herd”).

parole.significato: a deer, ruminant mammal of the family Cervidae
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hiorter, from Old Norse hjǫrtr, from Proto-Germanic *herutaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kerw-.

parole.significato: a wheel; a circular device capable of rotating on its axis
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hiul, hiughl, from Old Norse hvél, hjól, from Proto-Germanic *hwehwlą, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlóm, *kʷékʷlos (“wheel”).
From Old Swedish hiælmber, from Old Norse hjalmr (“helmet”), from Proto-Germanic *helmaz.

parole.significato: to help; give aid or assistance to
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hiælpa, from Old Norse hjalpa, from Proto-Germanic *helpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp-.

parole.significato: a hero, a person (of any sex) of great bravery
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæladhe (helade, hælædhe, hæladh, hælædh, hælæth, hælæd, heled, hælith, hellit, helte; influenced by Middle Low German helt, Old Saxon helith), potentially from an earlier Old Norse *hælaði, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *haliþaz. Assumed to have initially been borrowed from Old Sa

From Old Swedish hiærta, from Old Norse hjarta, from Proto-Germanic *hertô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”). Compare English heart, German Herz, Dutch hart, Icelandic, Faroese and Norwegian Nynorsk hjarta, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål hjerte.

parole.significato: hollow object; socket (like the shaft socket on a speartip)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish holker, from Old Norse holkr, from Proto-Germanic *hulkaz (“cavity, hollow, recess”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide, conceal”). Cognate with Icelandic hólkur, English hulk.

parole.significato: a small island, an islet, a holm (normally uninhabited and typically more or less covered with trees)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish holmber, Old Norse holmr, from Proto-Germanic *hulmaz. Cognate with Icelandic hólmur (dative hólmi), German Holm. (sense 3) is a semantic loan from Icelandic hólmur.

parole.significato: she; the third-person, singular, feminine pronoun in the nominative case
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hōn, from Old Norse hón, from Proto-Germanic *hēnō (compare *ainaz). Cognate with Icelandic hún, Danish hun and Norwegian Bokmål hun.
From Old Norse hunang, from Proto-Germanic *hunangą.
From Old Swedish hoppa, huppa, from Old Norse hoppa, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną, from Proto-Indo-European *kewb- (“to bend; a bend, joint”).

parole.significato: adultery, fornication (sex with someone who is not one's spouse, or sex between unmarried people – sexual immorality):…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hōr, from Old Norse hór, from Proto-Germanic *hōrą, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“loved”). Related to English whore.
From Old Swedish hōra, from Old Norse hóra, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“dear, loved”). Compare Danish hore, English whore, Dutch hoer, German Hure. Doublet of kär.
From Old Swedish hōsta, probably from the oblique case of Old Norse hósti, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstô.
From Old Swedish hōsta, from Old Norse hósta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstōną.
From Old Swedish hōt n, from Old Norse hót n pl, from Proto-Germanic *hwōtō (“threat”), cognate with Gothic 𐍈𐍉𐍄𐌰 f (ƕōta). Related to *hwētaną (“to attack, stab”).

From Old Norse hóta, derived from the noun hót n pl (“threat”) (cf. Swedish hot). It has replaced an older (now obsolete) verb, höta, from Old Norse hœta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōtijaną, cognate with Danish høde (archaic), Gothic 𐍈𐍉𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ƕōtjan).

parole.significato: a hoof (of an odd-toed ungulate, like a horse – compare klöv)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hōv, from Old Norse hófr, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. Cognate with Danish hov, English hoof, German Huf, Dutch hoef.
From Old Swedish hūþ, from Old Norse húð, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *kuHtis.

parole.significato: to strike with something sharp (to cut into pieces, sculpt, damage, or for any other purpose); to stab, to cut, to hew,…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hugga, from Old Norse hǫggva, from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kowH-.
From Old Swedish hulder, from Old Norse hollr, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz. Cognate with Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌻𐌸𐍃 (hulþs), Icelandic hollur.

parole.significato: wood, forest (of any size); (or strictly) coppice
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish hult, from Old Norse holt (“wood”), from Proto-Germanic *hultą (“wood”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat, break”). Cognate with English holt and German Holz. First attested in 1210–1216.

From Old Swedish humble, from Old Norse humli, humall, to a probable Proto-Germanic *humilô or thereof. Probably from Proto-Slavic *xъmelь Compare with Norwegian Bokmål humle, Faroese humli, humla, Icelandic humall.

From Old Swedish hunder, from Old Norse hundr, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwn̥tós, a variant of *ḱwṓ (“dog”). Masculine in Late Modern Swedish. Akin to Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍃 (hunds), English hound.
From Old Swedish hundraþ, from Old Norse hundrað, from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”).
From Old Norse hungr, from Proto-Germanic *hunhruz.
From Old Swedish hūs, from Old Norse hús, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą (“house”).

parole.significato: a hood, a bonnet, a cap, a tea cosy, a (soft and removable) cover
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hūva, from Old Norse húfa, from Proto-Germanic *hūbǭ.
From Old Swedish hovuþ, from Old Norse hǫfuð, from Proto-Germanic *hafudą or *habudą, northern form of *haubudą, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *kaput-.
From Old Norse hylla, from Proto-Germanic *hulþijaną, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz, (whence Swedish huld (“faithful, gracious, sweet”), Icelandic hollur (“loyal”)). Cognate with Icelandic hylla.
From Old Swedish hysa, from Old Norse hýsa, from Proto-Germanic *hūsijaną, equivalent to hus + -a. Cognate with Icelandic hýsa.

parole.significato: to blaspheme (express disdain for something considered holy)
parole.testo: Formed from the noun håd (“mockery”), from Old Swedish haþ, from Old Norse háð, from Proto-Germanic *hawiþą, related to *hauniz (“miserable”).

parole.significato: to stick (together), to attach, to adhere
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæpta, from Old Norse hepta, from Proto-Germanic *haftijaną. Cognate with Danish hæfte, Norwegian Norwegian hefta, Icelandic hepta, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐍆𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (haftjan), Old Saxon heftian, hehtian, Middle Low German and Dutch hechten, and German heften.
Inherited from Old Swedish hægger, from Old Norse heggr, from Proto-Germanic *hagô. Doublet of hage and häck. Compare English hedgeberry.
From Old Norse hæll, from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz.

From Old Swedish *hæla, probably to an Old Norse *hæla (with cognate Danish hæle), ultimately to a Proto-Germanic *helaną. Doublet of hölja. Compare Old Swedish hæle (“hidden spot”), hæl (“death, underworld”). Cognate of German hehlen, Dutch helen (“to fence”).

parole.significato: half, one of two roughly equal parts
parole.testo: From Old Norse helft, from Proto-Germanic *halbiþō.

parole.significato: a more or less flat, often sloping section of rock surface
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hal, from Old Norse hallr, from Proto-Germanic *halluz.
From Old Swedish hēlsa, from Old Norse heilsa, from Proto-Germanic *hailisōną, from *hailaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos.

parole.significato: to get, to fetch, to retrieve (go get and bring (back) somewhere)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæmta, from Old Norse heimta, from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną.

parole.significato: to happen; chiefly what happens quickly or for a short time
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hænda, from Old Norse henda, from Proto-Germanic *handijaną.
From Old Swedish hængia, from Old Norse hanga, from Proto-Germanic *hanhaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱenk-.

parole.significato: here; at this time or at this place
parole.testo: From Old Norse hér, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r.
Inherited from Old Swedish hærþa, from Old Norse herða, from Proto-Germanic *hardijaną.
From Old Swedish hæria, from Old Norse herja, from Proto-Germanic *harjōną. Derived from *harjaz (see här).
From Old Swedish härma, from Old Norse herma, from Proto-Germanic *harmijaną (“to repeat; to imitate”).

parole.significato: a horse; a large mammal, Equus caballus
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæster, from Old Norse hestr, from Proto-Germanic *hangistaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱanḱest-, *kankest-, see also German Hengst and Dutch hengst (“stallion”). The sense "heroin" is a calque from English "horse".
From Old Swedish hætta, Old Norse hetta, from Proto-Germanic *hattijǭ.

From Old Swedish hæfia, from Old Norse hefja, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyé-, from the root *kap- (“to seize”). Compare Danish hæve, Norwegian hevja, English heave, Dutch heffen, German heben. Doublet of hiva.
From Old Swedish hogher, from Old Norse hugr, from Proto-Germanic *hugiz.

parole.significato: a hole (opening straight through or partway through something)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hul, hol, from Old Norse hol, from Proto-Germanic *hulą, from Proto-Indo-European *kuH-, *kewH-.
From Old Swedish halda, halla, holda, holla, from Old Norse halda, from Proto-Germanic *haldaną. Further etymology uncertain; possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide, conceal”).
From Old Swedish hār, from Old Norse hár, from Proto-Germanic *hērą, from Proto-Indo-European *keres- (“rough hair, bristle”).
From Old Swedish harþer, from Old Norse harðr, from Proto-Germanic *harduz, from Proto-Indo-European *kert-, *kret- (“strong, powerful”).
From Old Swedish hø̄, from Old Norse hey, from Proto-Germanic *hawją.

parole.significato: high; tall; reaching a great distance from the ground or being found high above it
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hø̄gher, from Old Norse haugr, from Proto-Germanic *haugaz, variant of *hauhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-.
From Old Swedish hø̄gher, from Old Norse haugr, from Proto-Germanic *haugaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-.

parole.significato: right (opposite of left; on the east side when facing north)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hǿgri, comparative of hǿgr (“easy, convenient”), from Proto-Germanic *hōgiz (“skilled”). Cognate with Icelandic hægri, Danish højre and Norwegian høyre.

parole.significato: height, altitude, elevation (distance above the ground or another reference)
parole.testo: Corresponds to Old Norse hæð, from Proto-Germanic *hauhiþō. Compare Norwegian Bokmål høyde, Dutch hoogte, Old High German hohida, Gothic hauhiþa, English height.
From Old Swedish hø̄ker, from Old Norse haukr, from Proto-Germanic *habukaz, probably ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“seize”).
From Old Swedish hylia, from Old Norse hylja, from Proto-Germanic *huljaną.

From Old Swedish hø̄ra, from Old Norse heyra, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti.

parole.significato: a corner; the point where two converging lines meet; an angle, either external or internal.
parole.testo: From Old Norse hyrna, from Proto-Germanic *hurnijǭ.
From Old Norse hyrna, from Proto-Germanic *hurnijǭ.
From Old Swedish ī, īr, from Old Norse ír, variant of ér, from Proto-Germanic *jīz, variant of *jūz, from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs.

From Old Norse fjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *ferudi (“last year”), from Proto-Indo-European *peruti (“last year”, literally “on the other side of a year”). parole.significato: used to signify that an action is done with intensity
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ī, from Old Norse í, from Proto-Germanic *in.

parole.testo: From Old Swedish idhe, ydhe (“yew”), from Old Norse *iði, from *iðja (“greenery”, literally “yew + collective suffix”), from an earlier *īṷiþia, from Proto-Germanic *īwiþia, *īhwiþia, a collective form of *īhwaz (“yew”) + *-iþia (“collective suffix”).
