Compound of ide (“yew”) + gran (“spruce”), from Old Swedish idhe, yew, from Old Norse *iði, from *iðja (“greenery”, literally “yew + collective suffix”), from an earlier *īṷiþia, from Proto-Germanic *īwiþia, *īhwiþia, a collective form of *īhwaz (“yew”) + *-iþia (“collective suffix”). Compare Swedis
From i + från, from Old Norse frá, from Proto-Germanic *fram (“from”), from Proto-Germanic *framaz (“forth, forward”).
From Old Swedish igil, from Old Norse *igla, from Proto-Germanic *egulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ógʷʰis (“snake”). Cognate with Icelandic igla, Danish igle, Norwegian igle and German Egel.
From Old Norse inngangr, from Proto-Germanic *inngangaz. Equivalent to in- + gång.
From Old Swedish is, from Old Norse íss, from Proto-Germanic *īsą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyH-.

parole.significato: lard, grease; a solid but soft fat from the intestines of certain animals
parole.testo: From Old Swedish īster, from Old Norse ístr, from Proto-Germanic *instraz (“intestine”).
From Old Norse já, from Proto-Germanic *ja.

parole.significato: earth, soil; a rock- or sand-based unconsolidated material in which land plants grow
parole.testo: From Old Swedish iorþ, from Old Norse jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er-.

From Old Swedish iūl, from Old Norse jól, from Proto-Germanic *jehwlą. First attested in the late 13th century. Cognate with English Yule, Danish jul, Estonian jõulud, Finnish joulu, Faroese jól, Icelandic jól, Norwegian jul, and Scots Yule.

parole.significato: an udder (part of domestic milk-giving animal that expresses milk)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish iūwer, iūver (Early Old Swedish), iūger, iūgher (Late Old Swedish), from Old Norse júr, júgr, from Proto-Germanic *euduraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ewHdʰ-r̥- (“udder”).

From Old Swedish iæmpn, from Old Norse jafn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz. Compare Danish jævn, Norwegian Bokmål jevn, Norwegian Nynorsk jamn, Faroese javnur, Icelandic jafn, English even, Dutch even, effen, German eben.
From Old Swedish iæmpnt (“even”, adjective), neuter of iæmpn, from Old Norse jafn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz.
From Old Swedish iärpe, from Old Norse jarpi, from Old Norse jarpr (“brown”), from Proto-Germanic *erpaz (“light brown”).
From Old Swedish iæster, from Old Norse jǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *jestuz, from Proto-Indo-European *yes- (“to boil, to foam”).

parole.significato: jotun; a mythical humanoid creature, originally human-sized but later associated with great size
parole.testo: From, iætti, from Old Norse *iætti, byform of Old Norse jǫtunn, from Proto-Germanic *etunaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-. Doublet of (dialectal) jutul, juttul, jottel (“the devil; clever handy man, trixter, sly fox”); from Old Swedish *iatul, alternative form of iætun (“giant; jotun”); also borr

parole.significato: disqualification, challenge (judge's interest in the result of the case for which they should not be allowed to sit)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish iæf (“doubt”), from Old Norse ef (“doubt”), from Proto-Germanic *jabą, *ibą, whence Proto-Germanic *jabai (“if”), whence Icelandic ef (“if”) and Old English ġif (“if”).
From Old Swedish kaka, from Old Norse kaka, from Proto-Germanic *kakǭ (“cake”), from Proto-Indo-European *gog- (“ball-shaped object”).

parole.significato: lacking its natural covering; bare, without hair or vegetation or leaves or the like
parole.testo: From or related to Old Norse *kǫlr, from Proto-Germanic *kalwaz (“bare, bald”).
From Old Swedish kalder, kaller, from Old Norse kaldr, from Proto-Germanic *kaldaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gel-.

parole.significato: to call, denote, refer to; to give as a name
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kalla, from Old Norse kalla, from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną.

From Old Swedish kalver, from Old Norse kalfr (“calf”), from Proto-Germanic *kalbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷolbʰo- (“womb, animal young”). Compare Norwegian and Danish kalv, Icelandic kálfur, Dutch kalf, German Kalb, English calf.

From Old Swedish kamber, from Old Norse kambr, cognate with Danish kam and Dutch kam. That in turn derived from Proto-Germanic *kambaz, whence also Old English camb (English comb), Old High German kamb (German Kamm). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth (animate)”), whence also Ancie

parole.significato: to comb (to groom the hair with a toothed implement)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kamba, replaced older umlauted form kæmba under influence by the noun kamber (“comb”), from Old Norse kemba, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną. Compare Danish kæmme, Norwegian kjemme, Icelandic kemba.
From Old Norse ker, from Proto-Germanic *kazą.

parole.significato: to throw (make an object fly through the air)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kasta, from Old Norse kasta, from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Faroese, Icelandic, Norwegian Nynorsk kasta, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål kaste and English cast.

From the older form kavle, from Old Swedish kafle, kafli, from Old Norse kafli, from Proto-Germanic *kablaz (“round piece of wood”). Cognate to Norwegian Nynorsk kjevle, Norwegian Bokmål kjevle, Icelandic kefli.
From Old Swedish kiþ, from Old Norse kið, from Proto-Germanic *kidją‚ from Proto-Indo-European *gidʰ-.
From Old Norse kinn, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu- (“cheek”). Compare Danish kind, Norwegian and Icelandic kinn, German Kinn, Dutch kin, English chin.

parole.significato: a cauldron, a kettle (large cooking vessel)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ketill, from Proto-Germanic *katilaz, from Late Latin catillus.
From Old Swedish kitla, from Old Norse kitla, from Proto-Germanic *kitilōną, frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *kitōną (“to tickle”), from Proto-Indo-European *geid- (“to stick, jab, tickle”).
Inherited from Old Norse kífa, from Proto-Germanic *kībaną.
Inherited from Old Norse kífa, from Proto-Germanic *kībaną.
From klappa (“to clap”), from Old Norse klappa, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną.

parole.significato: to take one or more big steps, to step, to stride
parole.testo: From Old Swedish klīva, from Old Norse klífa, from Proto-Germanic *klībaną.
From Old Norse kló, from Proto-Germanic *klawō.
From Old Swedish klūter, from Old Norse klútr, from Proto-Germanic *klūtaz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål klut, Danish klud, English clout (“cloth”), Old English clūt. Compare with origin for klot.

parole.significato: a clove; a separate bulb of a garlic
parole.testo: From Old Norse kluft, klyft, from Proto-Germanic *kluftiz.
From Old Swedish klȳva, from Old Norse kljúfa, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną (“to cleave, split”), from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ-.
Inherited from Old Swedish klēngia, from Old Norse klengja, from Proto-Germanic *klangijaną. Doublet of klunga.
From Old Swedish klā, from Old Norse klá, from Proto-Germanic *klawjaną. Doublet of klia, klösa, klo, and klåda.
From Old Norse knappr, from Proto-Germanic *knappô, *knappa-, which is perhaps related to *knappō (“knob, boy”).
From Old Swedish knīver, from Old Norse knífr (“knife”), from Proto-Germanic *knībaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gneybʰ-.
From Old Swedish knōe, from Old Norse knúi, from Proto-Germanic *knūwan. See also Danish kno; further Swedish knoka, German Knochen, Dutch knook, knokkel, English knuckle.

parole.significato: a knot (loop, of for example a piece of string)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish knūter from Old Norse knútr, from Proto-Germanic *knuttô, *knudô (compare *knuttan-, whence English knot). Originally of corner joints of log cabins in (sense 2).
From Old Swedish knyta, from Old Norse knýta, from Proto-Germanic *knuttijaną, related to *knuttô.
From Old Norse kné, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu (“knee”).
From Old Swedish knodha, from Old Norse knoða, from Proto-Germanic *knudaną, compare dialectal knö.

parole.significato: to crowd, to jostle, to squeeze
parole.testo: From knå, a dialectal short form of standard Swedish knåda (“to knead”), with western Swedish vowel fronting /oː/ > /œː/, sometimes represented in dialectal writing with a circumflex ⟨ô⟩, compare gôr-. From Old Swedish knodha, from Old Norse knoða, from Proto-Germanic *knudaną.
From Old Norse ko, from East Old Norse ko, from Proto-Germanic *kōz.
From Old Norse kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷol-, from *ǵwelH- (“to burn, shine”).
From Old Swedish koma, from Old Norse koma, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem-. Etymology 1 sense 3 is probably a semantic loan from English come.

From Old Swedish kona, kuna (“woman, wife, concubine”) (genitive plural kvinna, kvænna), from Old Norse kona, from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ. Feminine in Late Modern Swedish. Doublet of kvinna. Akin to English quean.
From Old Swedish konunger, from Old Norse konungr (“king”), from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (“king”).

From Old Swedish korver, presumably from Old Norse kurfr, from Proto-Germanic *kurbiz. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kurv (with dialectal variants like korv and kørv), and English kerf. Attested since the first half of the 15th century.
From Old Swedish krabba, krabbe, from Old Norse krabbi, from Proto-Germanic *krabbô, from Proto-Indo-European *grobʰ- (“to crawl, scratch”). See also kräfta (“crayfish”).

parole.significato: force (similar senses to English, though less often of groups of people)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krapter, from Old Norse kraptr, krǫptr, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz.
From Old Norse krǫf f, from Proto-Germanic *krafō, related to Proto-Germanic *krafjaną (“to demand”).

From Old Norse krafla (compare Danish kravle (“to crawl, creep”), Swedish kräla (“to creep, crawl”)), from Proto-Germanic *krablōną (compare Saterland Frisian krabbelje, Dutch krabbelen, German Low German krabbeln, German krabbeln), frequentative of *krabbōną (“to scratch, scrape”). Compare also Sat
From Old Norse kringr, originally "turn or go about in circles," from Proto-Germanic *kringaz.

parole.significato: a hook (rod bent into a curved shape)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krōker, from Old Norse krókr, from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz.

parole.significato: a body (of a human, whether living or dead, like in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kropper, from Old Norse kroppr (“body”), from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz, from Proto-Indo-European *grewb-.
From Old Swedish krympa, from Old Norse krimpa (Compare Old West Norse kreppa), from Proto-Germanic *krimpaną.

From Old Swedish krȳpa, from Old Norse krjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *kreupaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“turn, wind”). Compare Norwegian krype, Danish krybe, Icelandic krjúpa, English creep, Dutch kruipen.

parole.significato: to tense the muscles of the abdomen in order to expel something (usually feces or a baby); to push, to bear down
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krȳsta, from Old Norse *krjósta, from Proto-Germanic *kreustaną (“to grind”).
From Old Swedish krängia, from Old Norse krinkr, from Proto-Germanic *kringaz (“circle, ring”).
From Old Swedish kræfia, from Old Norse krefja, from Proto-Germanic *krafjaną or Proto-Germanic *krabjaną. Cognate with Danish kræve, Norwegian Bokmål kreve, Old English crafian and English crave.

parole.significato: crow, especially hooded crow, Corvus cornix
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krāka, from Old Norse kráka, from Proto-Germanic *krakǭ, a derivative of *krakōną, from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”). Cognate to German krähe, English crow.
From Old Swedish kodde, from Old Norse koddi, from Proto-Germanic *kuddô, from Proto-Indo-European *gewt-.
From Old Norse kokkr, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz. Cognate with English cock.
From Old Norse kollr, from Proto-Germanic *kullaz.
Inherited from Old Swedish kumbel, from Old Norse kumbl, from Proto-Germanic *kumblą.
From contraction of konung, from Old Swedish konunger, from Old Norse konungr, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (“king”).
From Old Swedish kunna, from Old Norse kunna, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-.
From Old Swedish qval, from Old Norse kvǫl, from Proto-Germanic *kwalō. Cognate of German Qual, Dutch kwaal, Old English cwalu. Compare origin of kvälja.
From Old Norse kvirr, kyrr, from Proto-Germanic *kwerruz.
From Old Swedish quaster, from Old Norse *kvǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *kwastuz.
From Old Swedish qviþer (“belly, stomach, womb”), from Old Norse kviðr, from Proto-Germanic *kweþuz. Cognate with Icelandic kviður, Old English cwiþ, Gothic 𐌵𐌹𐌸𐌿𐍃 (qiþus).

From Old Swedish qvikker, qviker, from Old Norse kvikr (whence also Norwegian Bokmål kvikk, Norwegian Nynorsk kvik, Icelandic kvikur and Faroese kvikur), from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz, whence also English quick. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).
From Old Swedish qvikna, from Old Norse kvikna, from Proto-Germanic *kwiknaną.
From Old Swedish kvinna, from Runic Swedish kuino, from Old Norse kvæna, from kván (“wife”), from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn. Cognate with English queen.
From Old Swedish kvæþa, from Old Norse kveða, from Proto-Germanic *kweþaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-. Cognate with English quoth, Icelandic kveða.

parole.significato: lay, poem, song (used mostly in reference to Old Norse poetry)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kvæþe, from Old Norse kvæði, from Proto-Germanic *kwēþiją.
From Old Swedish qvælia, from Old Norse kvelja, from Proto-Germanic *kwaljaną. Compare Old Armenian կեղ (keł).
From Old Swedish quæld, qvælder, from Old Norse kveld, from Proto-Germanic *kwildiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-.

parole.significato: to chill, to cool, to refrigerate; to lower the temperature of something
parole.testo: From Old Norse kœla, from Proto-Germanic *kōlijaną.
From Old Swedish kus, kos, from Old Norse koss, from Proto-Germanic *kussaz. Cognate with English kiss, German Kuss, Icelandic koss.

parole.significato: to kiss passionately or with great affection (compare with pussa), to snog (UK)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kyssa, from Old Norse kyssa, from Proto-Germanic *kussijaną.
From Old Swedish kænna, from Old Norse kenna, from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną.
Inherited from Old Swedish käril, from Old Norse kerald (“container”), from Proto-Germanic *kazą. Doublet of kar.

parole.significato: a seed (of a fruit, nut, berry, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kiærne, from Old Norse kjarni, from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“core, kernel”). Cognate with Icelandic kjarni, German Kern, Dutch kern, Luxembourgish Kär.

parole.significato: a churn (a vessel used for churning, especially for producing butter)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kerna, from Old Norse kirna, from Proto-Germanic *kernǭ. Cognate with Icelandic kirna, English churn, German Karn, Dutch karn, West Frisian tsjerne.

From Old Norse kjarr (“copsewood, underbrush, bushes, scrub”), from Proto-Germanic *kerzą, *kerzuz (“scrub, bushes”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵers- (“to turn, bend, twist”). From Old Swedish kāter, from Old Norse kátr, from Proto-Germanic *kanhtaz. Cognate with Danish kåd, Norwegian Bokmål kåt and Norwegian Nynorsk kåt. Possibly also related to Latin gaudeō (“to rejoice”).

From Old Swedish køn, kyn, from Old Norse kyn, from Proto-Germanic *kunją, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to produce”). Cognate with English kin, Danish køn, Norwegian kjønn, Icelandic kyn, Dutch kunne, Gothic 𐌺𐌿𐌽𐌹 (kuni), and the borrowed Finnish word kunnia.

From Old Swedish kø̄pa, from Old Norse keypa, kaupa, from Proto-Germanic *kaupijaną, *kaupōną (“to buy, trade”), from *kaupô (“innkeeper, merchant”), Latin caupo (“innkeeper, shopkeeper, tradesman”), caupōnor (“to trade, haggle”). From Old Swedish kø̄ra, from Old Norse keyra (“to drive, fling, toss”), from Proto-Germanic *kaurijaną, *karjaną (“to turn, sweep”). More at cair.
From Old Swedish køt, kiøt, from Old Norse kjǫt, from Proto-Germanic *ketwą. Cognate with Danish kød, Norwegian kjøtt, kjøt, Faroese kjøt, Icelandic kjöt.
From Old Norse hlaða, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂-. See also lada (“barn”).

parole.significato: a water-based solution of sugar, salt and/or other spices; e.g. brine
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lagher, from Old Norse lǫgr, from Proto-Germanic *laguz, from Proto-Indo-European *lókus. Cognate with Latin lacus.
From Old Norse lagg (“barrel stave, split piece of wood”), from Proto-Germanic *lawwd, from Proto-Indo-European *lewH- (“to sever, cut apart, loosen”).

parole.significato: lame, unable to move any limbs
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lamber, from Old Norse lami, from Proto-Germanic *lamaz.
From Old Swedish lamb, from Old Norse lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁l̥h₁onbʰos.

parole.significato: a country, a land (independent political entity)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish land, from Old Norse land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”).

parole.significato: habit which is difficult to get rid of, vice
parole.testo: From Old Swedish laster (Old Icelandic lǫstr), from Old Norse löstr, from the root of Proto-Germanic *lahaną (“to reproach, blame”), see also Old High German lastar (“vice”).
From Old Swedish later, from Old Norse latr, from Proto-Germanic *lataz, from Proto-Indo-European *lē(y)d-.

From Old Norse lax, from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz. The 1000 SEK sense probably refers to the salmon color of old 1000 SEK banknotes. From Old Swedish lēia, lea, from Old Norse hlæja (“to laugh”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną.
Inherited from Old Swedish lēþer, from Old Norse leiðr, from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyt-.

parole.significato: joint; the part of a limb where it can bend; such as a knee or a wrist; phalanx
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish liþer, from Old Norse liðr, from Proto-Germanic *liþuz.

parole.significato: track, route or way, along which one may walk, go by bicycle or drive a motor vehicle
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish lēþ, from Old Norse leið, from Proto-Germanic *laidō.

parole.significato: to (gently) lead; to guide, to conduct
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lēþa, from Old Norse leiða, from Proto-Germanic *laidijaną.
From Old Norse liðugr, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz.
From Old Swedish legha, lægha, from Old Norse lega, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną (“to lie; to rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”). Doublet of lager and läger.
From Old Swedish lēgha, from Old Norse leiga (“hire, rent, pay”), from Proto-Germanic *laigǭ (“loan”), from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave”). Cognate of Danish leie. Doublet of lån and län.
From Old Swedish leghia, from Old Norse leiga, from Proto-Germanic *laigijaną (“to lend”).
From Old Swedish lēka, from Old Norse leika, from Proto-Germanic *laikaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

From Old Swedish līkami, līkamber, from Old Norse líkami, líkamr, from Proto-Germanic *līkahamô. Cognate with Icelandic líkami, Danish legeme, Dutch lichaam, German Leichnam. The final -n originally comes from the definite article.

parole.significato: a limb (major appendage of a human or animal)
parole.testo: From Old Norse limr, from Proto-Germanic *limuz (“branch, limb”) (compare English limb).
From Old Norse linr, from Proto-Germanic *linwaz.

parole.significato: search; look throughout (a place) for something
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lēta, from Old Norse leita, from Proto-Germanic *wlaitōną.
From Old Swedish lever, from Old Norse hleifr, from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz. Cognate with Icelandic hleifur, English loaf, German Laib.
From Old Norse lyf, from Proto-Germanic *lubją. Doublet of lövja (“medicine”).

parole.significato: to live, to be alive (concretely or figuratively)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish liva, from Old Norse lifa, from Proto-Germanic *libjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, cling, linger”). Cognate with Norwegian leve, Danish leve, Icelandic lifa, Dutch leven, German leben and English live.
From Old Swedish lēva, from Old Norse leifa, from Proto-Germanic *laibijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, cling, linger”). Cognate with Icelandic leifa, English leave.
From Old Norse lifr, from Proto-Germanic *librō, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to smudge, stick”), from *ley- (“to be slimy, be sticky, glide”).
Inherited from Old Swedish liþ, from Old Norse hlíð, from Proto-Germanic *hlīdō. Cognate of Latin clīvus, Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma), Old English hliþ.
From Old Swedish līþa, from Old Norse líða, from Proto-Germanic *līþaną.

parole.significato: a scythe (instrument for mowing grass, grain, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish līe, lē, from Old Norse lé, from Proto-Germanic *lewô, from Proto-Indo-European *leu- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: to lie; be in a horizontal position
parole.testo: From Old Swedish liggia, from Old Norse liggja, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.

parole.significato: looking like, resembling (in appearance or other characteristics)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish līker, from Old Norse líkr, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.
Inherited from Old Swedish lik, from Old Norse lík, from Proto-Germanic *līką, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

parole.significato: to the same degree, as, equally
parole.testo: From Old Norse líka, from Proto-Germanic *līkāną, *galīkāną.
From Old Norse lín, from Proto-Germanic *līną. Cognate with English linen.

parole.significato: a wire, a rope, a line
parole.testo: From Old Norse lína, from Proto-Germanic *līnǭ (“line, rope, flaxen cord, thread”), from *līną (“flax”). Hypothetised to be derived from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”), although it's impossible to reconstruct a common PIE protoform due to discrepancies with other European branches and absence o
Inherited from Old Swedish lind, from Old Norse lind, from Proto-Germanic *lindō.

parole.significato: broad white cloth (particularly ones used for swaddling)
parole.testo: Oblique form of linde, from Old Swedish linde, lindi, from Old Norse lindi (“belt; girdle; sash; wrap”), likely related to Proto-Germanic *linþaz.
From Old Swedish list, from Old Norse list, from Proto-Germanic *listiz, from Proto-Indo-European *leys-, *leyǝs-. Cognate with Icelandic list.
From Old Norse hlíta, from a fusion of Proto-Germanic *wlītaną (“to see”) and a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (“to lean”).
From Old Norse lítinn, accusative of lítill, from Proto-Germanic *lītilaz.
From Old Swedish līf, from Old Norse líf, from Proto-Germanic *lībą.
From Old Swedish liuþ, from Old Norse hljóð, from Proto-Germanic *hleuþą. Cognate with Faroese ljóð, Norwegian lyd and ljod, Danish lyd, Icelandic hljóð, German Laut, Scots luid, Dutch luid.

parole.significato: to lie, to tell an untruth
parole.testo: From Old Swedish liūgha, from Old Norse ljúga, from Proto-Germanic *leuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to tell a lie”). Cognate with Danish lyve, Faroese ljúgva (whence lúgva), Icelandic ljúga, Norwegian Bokmål lyve and Norwegian Nynorsk ljuga.
From Old Swedish liūs, from Old Norse ljóss, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-so-, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-.
From Old Swedish liūs, from Old Norse ljós, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-so-m, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-.
By surface analysis, ljuv + -lig. Diachronically, from Old Norse ljúfligr, from Proto-Germanic *leubalīkaz.
Inherited from Old Swedish lō, from Old Norse lóa, derived from or related to Proto-Germanic *luhsaz.

parole.significato: a lock of hair, a curl of hair
parole.testo: From Old Norse lok, lokkr, from Proto-Germanic *lukkaz.

parole.significato: to attract, to lure, to entice
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lokka, lukka (“to kindly persuade”), from Old Norse lokka (“to lure, entice”), from Proto-Germanic *lukkōną (“to allure”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to lie”). Cognate with Icelandic lokka, Danish lokke.

parole.significato: a part, a share, a piece, a portion (of a heritage, a lottery, of land, of fate)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish luter, loter, from Old Norse hlutr, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą, from Proto-Indo-European *klew-.
From Old Swedish luta, lota, from Old Norse hluta, from Proto-Germanic *hlutōną.
From Old Swedish lof, from Old Norse lof, from Proto-Germanic *lubą.
From Old Swedish lova, from Old Norse lofa, from Proto-Germanic *lubōną, equivalent to lov + -a. Cognate with Danish love, Norwegian love, Dutch loven, German loben.

parole.significato: a gap, a hole, an open slot, a small empty room
parole.testo: From Old Swedish loka, luka, from Old Norse lúka, from Proto-Germanic *lūkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *lewg-. Compare English lock.
From Old Norse loðinn, from Proto-Germanic *ludanaz, past participle of *leudaną (“to sprout, to grow”).

parole.significato: lung (organ that extracts oxygen from the air)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lunga, from Proto-Germanic *lungw- (literally “the light organ”), from Proto-Indo-European *lengʷʰ- (“light, agile, nimble”). Compare Danish and Norwegian lunge, Icelandic lunga, German Lunge, lung.

From lunga (“lung”) + sot (“disease, sickness”). It should be noted that sot here is an archaic word for disease or sickness, inherited from Old Norse sótt, from Proto-Germanic *suhtiz. It is thus not related to the meaning of soot, which instead comes from Old Norse sót, from Proto-Germanic *sōtą.

parole.significato: a simple, straight horn (used as an instrument or for signaling)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lūdher (“horn, trumpet”), from Old Norse lúðr, from Proto-Germanic *lawwō, from Proto-Indo-European *lowH-éh₂.
From Old Swedish lūs, from Old Norse lús, from Proto-Germanic *lūs, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *luHs-, *lewH-.
From Old Swedish lusta, from Old Norse *lusta, from Proto-Germanic *lustōną.
From Old Swedish lūta, from Old Norse lúta, from Proto-Germanic *lūtaną.

parole.significato: to close (a door, gate, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lykja (preterit lukta), from Proto-Germanic *lukjaną (“to close, shut”).
From Old Swedish lyþa, from Old Norse hlýða, from Proto-Germanic *hliuþijaną.

parole.significato: to lift; to move something upwards
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lypta, from Old Norse lypta, Proto-Germanic *luftijaną.
From Old Swedish lykt, a deverbal from lūka (“to close, to shut”), from Old Norse lúka, from Proto-Germanic *lūkaną.
Present of obsolete lysta, from Old Norse lysta, Proto-Germanic *lustijaną. Related to lust.

parole.significato: lee (the state of not being windy due to something blocking the wind), (as a more common translation) shelter
parole.testo: From Old Norse hlé, from Proto-Germanic *hlewą.

parole.significato: a leak; a crack, crevice, fissure, or hole which admits water or other fluid, or lets it escape.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish læka, from Old Norse leka, from Proto-Germanic *lekaną.

parole.significato: leather (material produced by tanning animal skin)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lædher (“leather”), from Old Norse leðr (“leather”), from Proto-Germanic *leþrą.

From Old Norse legr, from Proto-Germanic *legrą, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to be situated, lie”). Related to ligga (“to lie”), lägga (“to lay”) and läge (“position”). Doublet of lager (“store”), derived through German Lager.
From Old Swedish lægger, from Old Norse leggr, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(ǝ)lak-, *lēk-.

parole.significato: to place lying (to lay) somewhere, to place/put in a lying position (not in a standing position); in particular used li…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish læggia, from Old Norse leggja, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaną. Causative of *ligjaną (see ligga).
From Old Norse lækna, from Proto-Germanic *lēkinōną. Cognate with Icelandic lækna.

From late Old Swedish lǣkiare, remade (by way of the agent suffix -are) from earlier Old Swedish lǣkir, from (east) Old Norse *lækir (cf. Old West Norse læknir), from Proto-Germanic *lēkijaz. Equivalent to läka (“heal”) + -are (“-er”). Identical in formation to Norwegian Nynorsk lækjar and Proto-Sla

parole.significato: to leave; to not take away with oneself but leave as available for others; to deposit
parole.testo: From earlier lemna, from Old Swedish limna, lifna, from Old Norse lifna, inchoative of Proto-Germanic *lībaną (“to remain, to be left”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp-.
From Old Norse lengd, from Proto-Germanic *langiþō.

parole.significato: a link (in a chain or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lænker, from Old Norse *hlenkr (cf. Old West Norse hlekkr), from Proto-Germanic *hlankiz.
From Old Swedish lærikia, from Old Norse lævirki, from Proto-Germanic *laiwazikǭ.
From Old Swedish læsa, from Old Norse lesa, from Proto-Germanic *lesaną, from Proto-Indo-European *les-.
From Old Norse leistr, from Proto-Germanic *laistiz, from Proto-Indo-European *leys- (“track, furrow”). Cognate with English last.
From Old Swedish lǣtter, from Old Norse léttr, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-.

parole.significato: low, short; having a small height
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lāgher, from Old Norse lágr, from Proto-Germanic *lēgaz, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”).

parole.significato: a flame (burning), a blaze, a flare
parole.testo: From Old Swedish loghi, lughi, from Old Norse logi, from Proto-Germanic *lugô. Related to Icelandic logi, Middle High German lohe, more distantly to Latin lucere (“to shine, to light”), Ancient Greek λευκός (leukós, “white”). All ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European *lewk-.
From Old Swedish lan, from Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-.
From Old Swedish langer, from Old Norse langr, from Proto-Germanic *langaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos. Compare English long, Dutch lang, German lang.
From Old Swedish lar, from Old Norse lær, from Proto-Germanic *lahwaz.
From Old Norse láss, from Proto-Germanic *lamsaz.

From Old Swedish lāta, from Old Norse láta, from Proto-Germanic *lētaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d- (“to let (go), be tired”). The sense “to sound” was also present in Old Norse and can be derived from the sense “to let (sound) go”.
From Old Norse lauðr, from Proto-Germanic *lauþrą, from Proto-Indo-European *lówh₃trom (“that which is used for washing”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash, bathe”).
From Old Swedish lø̄gh, from Old Norse laug, from Proto-Germanic *laugō.
From Old Swedish lœgha, from Old Norse lauga, from Proto-Germanic *laugō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃-. Cognate of Icelandic lauga.

parole.significato: contemptuous glee (at something or someone considered ridiculous), ridicule
parole.testo: Old Swedish löghe, from Old Norse hlœgi (“ridicule”), from Proto-Germanic *hlōgijaną (“to make laugh”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną (“to laugh”). Compare Danish løjer, Icelandic hlægja.

parole.significato: reward, something given to someone for a deed or achievement
parole.testo: From Old Swedish løn, from Old Norse laun, from Proto-Germanic *launą, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w-.
From Old Norse laun (“secrecy, concealment”), from Proto-Germanic *laugnaz (“hidden”).
From Old Norse laun (“secrecy, concealment”), from Proto-Germanic *laugnaz (“hidden”).
From Old Swedish lø̄pa, from Old Norse hlaupa, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną, from Proto-Indo-European *klewb- (“to spring, stumble”).

parole.significato: loose; not tightened, able to move
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lø̄s, from Old Norse lauss, from Proto-Germanic *lausaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁-.
From Old Swedish lø̄sa, from Old Norse leysa, from Proto-Germanic *lausijaną.
From Old Swedish lø̄sn, from Old Norse lausn from Proto-Germanic *lausīniz. Cognate of Danish løsen and Icelandic lausn.

parole.significato: a leaf (on a tree or bush and not a needle)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish løf, from Old Norse lauf, from Proto-Germanic *laubą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewp- (“peel, break off”).

parole.significato: A remedy or potion; a medicine.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lifia, lūfia, from Old Norse lyf, from Proto-Germanic *lubją. Doublet of lev (“spell; potion”).
From Old Norse maðra, from Proto-Germanic *madarǭ.
From Old Swedish maghi, from Old Norse magi, from Proto-Germanic *magô, from Proto-Indo-European *mak-, *maks-.
From Old Swedish magher, from Old Norse magr (“thin, meager”), from Proto-Germanic *magraz, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós.
From Old Swedish maka, oblique form of maki, from Old Norse maki, from Proto-Germanic *makô. Doublet of make. Because of the -a usually interpreted as feminine.

parole.significato: a spouse, a husband, a married man (mostly referring to a specific relation)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish maki, from Old Norse maki, from Proto-Germanic *makô. Doublet of maka.
From Old Swedish mala, from Old Norse mala, from Proto-Germanic *malaną.

Inherited from Old Norse malmr, from Proto-Germanic *malmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind”). First attested in 1286. Area outside main city center sense: originally referring to the two sandy hills north and south of Stockholm (see: Norrmalm and Södermalm), which would become part of
From Old Norse malt, from Proto-Germanic *maltą.
From Old Swedish maþer, mander, from Old Norse maðr, from Proto-Germanic *mann-.

parole.significato: mane (of a horse or lion or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish man, from Old Norse mǫn, from Proto-Germanic *manō.

parole.significato: a mythological creature blamed for giving people nightmares
parole.testo: From Old Norse mara, from Proto-Germanic *marǭ; cognate to Old English mare or mære.

parole.significato: ground (surface of the Earth (or some other planet, etc.), or the area (immediately) beneath it)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mark, from Old Norse mǫrk, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary, border”). Cognate with Latin margo (“border, edge”)―and hence English margin―and also with Old Irish mruig, bruig (“border, march”).

parole.significato: a stitch, a mesh (space enclosed by threads)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mǫskvi, mǫskun, from Proto-Germanic *maskwǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *mozgo-.
From Old Norse matr, from Proto-Germanic *matiz, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d-. Cognate with English meat.
From Old Swedish mæþ, from Old Norse með, from Proto-Germanic *midi.

parole.significato: while; during the same time that
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mæþan, mædhan, from Old Norse meðan, from Proto-Germanic *medanō.

parole.significato: a handicap, long-time remnant of a physical or mental injury, which affects a person negatively
parole.testo: From Old Norse mein, from Proto-Germanic *mainą (“damage, hurt”), cognate with Icelandic mein, Norwegian mein, Old Saxon mēn, Old English mān; cognate with Icelandic meinn (“which causes injury”), Old English mǣne (“evil, deceptive”, adjective), Lithuanian maĭnas (“change”, noun), Proto-Slavic *měna

From Old Swedish mēnēþer, from Old Norse meineiðr, from Proto-Germanic *mainaiþaz (“perjury”), from *mainą + *aiþaz. Equivalent to men + ed. Cognate of Old English mānāþ, Danish mened, German Meineid, Dutch meineed.
From Old Norse meiri, from Proto-Germanic *maizô.

parole.significato: waist (part of the body between the pelvis and the stomach)
parole.testo: From Old Norse miðja, Proto-Germanic *midjǭ (“centre”), *midją.
From Old Swedish mīgha, from Old Norse míga, from Proto-Germanic *mīganą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃méyǵʰeti, from the root *h₃meyǵʰ- (“to urinate”).
From Old Swedish milder, from Old Norse mildr, from Proto-Germanic *mildijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *meldʰ-.
From Old Norse mínn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *méynos.
From Old Norse minni, from Proto-Germanic *minnizô.
From Old Norse *minska, from Proto-Germanic *minnisōną. More at mince.

parole.significato: to miss; to fail to hit (a target)
parole.testo: From Old Norse missa, from Proto-Germanic *missijaną. Doublet of mista.

parole.significato: lighter fog (cloud that forms at a low altitude and obscures vision)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mistr, from Proto-Germanic *mihstaz.
From Old Swedish miūker, from Old Norse mjúkr, from Proto-Germanic *meukaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mewg-.
From Old Swedish miielte, from Old Norse milti, from Proto-Germanic *miltiją.
From Old Swedish miödher, from Old Norse mjǫðr, from Proto-Germanic *meduz, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“sweet drink”).

parole.significato: flour; ground or milled grain or cereal, in particular of wheat
parole.testo: From Old Swedish miøl, from Old Norse mjǫl, from Proto-Germanic *melwą, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-. Cognate with English meal.

From Old Swedish miolk, from Old Norse mjǫlk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-. Cognate with Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌻𐌿𐌺𐍃 (miluks), Faroese mjólk, Icelandic mjólk, Norwegian Bokmål melk, mjølk, Norwegian Nynorsk mjølk, Danish mælk, English milk, Dutch melk, Dutch Low Saxon melk, Germa
From Old Norse móðr, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mō-, *mē-.
Derived from Old Norse móðir, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.

From Old Swedish moin, moghin, from Old Norse móa (“to digest”), from Proto-Germanic *meuk- *mūk-, from Proto-Indo-European *mewg- (“slimy, slippery”), see also Gothic 𐌼𐌿𐌺𐌰𐌼𐍉𐌳𐌴𐌹 (mukamōdei, “gentleness”). Corresponding to Danish moden, probably the past participle of a verb.
Short form of moder, from Old Norse móðir, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
From Old Norse morð, from Proto-Germanic *murþą, from Proto-Indo-European *mṛtóm.
Inherited from Old Swedish morghon, Old Norse morgunn, morginn, from Proto-Germanic *murginaz, from Proto-Indo-European *merkʷ-, *merǝkʷ-.
From Old Norse *mós, from Proto-Germanic *mōsą (“mush, porridge”).

parole.significato: A point where two or more objects meet (e.g. the joint of two bones).
parole.testo: From Old Norse mót, from Proto-Germanic *mōtą, *gamōtą. Interchange sense coined by Swedish professor in Nordic languages Ture Johannisson in 1956.
From Old Norse mold, from Proto-Germanic *muldō (“dirt, soil”). Cognate with Icelandic mold, German Mull, Dutch moude and Gothic 𐌼𐌿𐌻𐌳𐌰 (mulda).
From Old Swedish munder, from Old Norse muðr, munnr, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ment-.

parole.significato: mouse; small rodent of the genus Mus; especially species Mus musculus
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mūs, from Old Norse mús, from Proto-Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Indo-European *muh₂s (“mouse”). The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.
From Old Norse mikinn, accusative of mikill, from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂-.

Originally neuter singular of mycken, from Old Swedish mykin, mikin, accusative singular of mikil, from Old Norse mikill, from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz (“great, many”), from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“big, great”).
From Old Swedish mȳra, from Old Norse *mýra, from Proto-Germanic *miurijǭ (“ant”), from Proto-Indo-European *mowro-, *morwi (“ant”). Cognate with Icelandic maur.
From Old Swedish mæla, from Old Norse mæla, from Proto-Germanic *maþlijaną.

From Old Norse mergr, from Proto-Germanic *mazgaz < *mazgą, from Proto-Indo-European *mosgʰos. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk merg, Norwegian Bokmål marg, Danish marv, Icelandic mergur, Dutch merg, German Mark, English marrow.
From Old Swedish mærki, from Old Norse merki, from Proto-Germanic *markō (“boundary; boundary marker”), from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary, border”).
From Old Norse merr, from Proto-Germanic *marhijō.

parole.significato: to measure (determine a measurement with respect to some unit)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mæta, from Old Norse meta, from Proto-Germanic *metaną, from Proto-Indo-European *med-.
Apocopic form of måga, from Old Swedish magha, from Old Norse mega, from Proto-Germanic *maganą, from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe, from root *megʰ-.
From Old Swedish māgher, from Old Norse mágr, from Proto-Germanic *mēgaz.
From Old Norse mál (“language, speech, matter, affair, case”) (from Proto-Germanic *maþlą).

parole.significato: target; what one aims to hit
parole.testo: From Old Norse mál (“size, measurement, time, meal”), from Proto-Germanic *mēlą.
From Old Norse mánaðr, from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþs (“month”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). See also måne.
Inherited from Old Norse munu, from Proto-Germanic *munaną. Doublet of månne and månntro.
From Old Swedish manger, margher, marghin, from Old Norse mangr, margr, from Proto-Germanic *managaz.
mång- (“many”) + -fald (“-fold”). From Old Swedish mangfalder, from Old Norse margfaldr, from Proto-Germanic *managafalþaz.
From Old Norse mǫrðr, from Proto-Germanic *marþuz.
From Old Norse máttr, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz, *mahtuz. Cognate with Icelandic máttur, Faroese máttur, Norwegian Nynorsk mått, English might. Doublet of makt.
From Old Norse mœr, mær, from Proto-Germanic *mawī, from Proto-Indo-European *magʰ-.

parole.significato: to hurt, to make an effort that hurts, to bother (someone with something)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mœða (“to make weary, to exhaust; plague”), from Proto-Germanic *mōþijaną (“to make weary”), in turn from *mōþuz (“tired, weary”).
From Old Norse meyrr, from Proto-Germanic *marwaz.

parole.significato: dark (having an absolute or relative lack of light)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish myrker, mørker, from Old Norse myrkr, from Proto-Germanic *merkuz. Cognate with English murk.

parole.significato: darkness (a complete or (more often) partial absence of light, or figuratively)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish myrker, mørker, from Old Norse myrkr, from Proto-Germanic *merkuz.
From Old Swedish mø̄ta, from Old Norse mœta (“to meet”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną.

parole.significato: a meeting (gathering for a purpose, to discuss, make decisions, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mót, from Proto-Germanic *mōtą, *gamōtą.

parole.significato: back of the neck, nape (compare hals)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nakke, from Old Norse hnakki, from Proto-Germanic *hnakkô, from Proto-Indo-European *knog-, *kneg- (“back of the head, nape, neck”), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“to press, pinch, buckle, kink”). Cognate with English neck.
From Old Norse nagl (“nail”), from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-.
From Old Norse nakinn, nǫkkviðr (“naked”), from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós (“naked, bare”).

parole.significato: name (of a person or something else)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nampn, namn, from, Old Norse nafn, from Proto-Germanic *namô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.
Inherited from Old Swedish napper (“cup; bowl”), from Old Norse hnappr, from Proto-Germanic *hnappaz.

parole.significato: to take the bait, to bite (of a fish)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish nappa, from Old Norse *hnappa, from Proto-Germanic *hnappōną. Possibly related to näpen and näpsa.
Inherited from Old Swedish nāt, from Old Norse nátt, from Proto-Germanic *nahts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
From Old Norse niðr, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter. Cognates include English nether, Faroese and Icelandic niður, German nieder and Dutch neder.
From Old Swedish niþan, näþan, from Old Norse neðan (“below, beneath”), from Proto-Germanic *niþanē (“below, beneath”). Cognate to German nieden, Old English neoþan.
From Old Swedish niþer, nedher, from Old Norse niðr, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter.
From Old Swedish næi, from Old Norse nei, from Proto-Germanic *nai (“never”), *nē (“not”), from Proto-Indo-European *né, *nē, *nēy (negative particle).
A contraction of earlier neder, from Old Norse niðr, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter.

Since 1661, through rebracketing of the 2nd plural verb suffix -(e)n and the older pronoun I ("ye"), e.g. vissten I > visste ni (“did you know”). Compare Icelandic þér and þið which developed similarly. The Old Swedish ī, īr derives from Old Norse *īʀ (East Norse variant of ér) from Proto-Germanic *
Inherited from Old Swedish nidh, from Old Norse níð, from Proto-Germanic *nīþą. Cognate of Danish nid (Old Danish nith), Icelandic níð, Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐌹𐌸 (neiþ), German Neid, Dutch nijd.
From Old Swedish nīgha, from Old Norse hníga, from Proto-Germanic *hnīwaną.

From Old Swedish næmber (“apt, docile”), from Old Norse næmr, from Proto-Germanic *nāmjaz, derived from Proto-Germanic *nemaną (“to take”). Compare Danish Danish nem (“easy”) and Icelandic næmur (“docile, sensitive”).
From Old Norse nema, from Proto-Germanic *nemaną. Although this verb originally belonged to the class 4 of strong verbs, it has merged into class 3, possibly analogically to simma.

From Old Swedish nio, from Old Norse níu (whence also Danish and Norwegian ni, Icelandic níu, Faroese níggju) from Proto-Germanic *newun, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognates with Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌿𐌽 (niun); Old English niġon (English nine); Old Frisian nigun (West Frisian njoggen); Old High German n
From Old Swedish niundi, from Old Norse níundi, from Proto-Germanic *newundô.
From Old Swedish nitan, nittān, from Old Norse nítján, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun.
Inherited from Old Norse hnøggr, from Proto-Germanic *hnawwaz. Compare English niggardly. Likely unrelated to Finnish niukka.
From Old Swedish niūre, from Old Norse nýra, from Proto-Germanic *neurô, from Proto-Indo-European *negʷʰrós.
Old Swedish niūta, from Old Norse njóta, from Proto-Germanic *neutaną.
From Old Norse nóg, nógr, gnógr, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₂nóḱe (“he has reached, attained”), perfective of *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).

parole.significato: a pill, a bobble (ball of fibers formed on the surface of a textile)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish noppa, from Old Norse *hnoppa, from Proto-Germanic *hnuppô.
From Old Norse norðr, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą.

parole.significato: north; one of the four major compass points
parole.testo: From nord (influenced by norra), from Old Norse norðr, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą.

parole.significato: a nose of an animal (compare näsa)
parole.testo: From Old Norse nǫs, from Proto-Germanic *nasō, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Doublet of näsa.
From Old Swedish nōt, from Old Norse nót, from Proto-Germanic *nōtō. Related to nät (“net”).
From Old Swedish nū, Old Norse nú, from Proto-Germanic *nu.
From Old Norse nýr, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *néwyos (“new”).

From Old Swedish nykil, lykil, from Old Norse lykill, from Proto-Germanic *lukilaz, from Proto-Germanic *lūkaną (“close”) + an instrumental suffix -il-. The n-sound has developed through dissimilation of l-l. Related to English lock, Swedish lock, lucka.

parole.significato: a pinch, a dash; a small amount of powder or granules
parole.testo: From Old Swedish niūpa, from Old Norse *hnjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *hneupaną (“to pluck”). Related to Gothic 𐌳𐌹𐍃𐌷𐌽𐌹𐌿𐍀𐌰𐌽 (dishniupan, “to break apart”).

From Old Swedish hiupon (possibly nominative plural), from Old Norse *hjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *heupǭ. Compare Danish hyben, Norwegian nype, hjupa, Old Saxon hiopo, Old High German hiufo, dialectal German hiefen, hüfen, Old English héope and English hip. The initial n- is the product of metanalysi
From Old Swedish niūsa, from Old Norse hnjósa, from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną.
From Old Norse nebbi, from Proto-Germanic *nabją. Further origin unknown.

parole.significato: A Näcken, a nix (noun contra proper noun); a male water-spirit in human form, mainly residing in rivers and lakes, who…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish neker, näkker, from Old Norse nykr, from Proto-Germanic *nikwiz-, ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *neygʷ- (“wash”, verb). First attested in 1430. Cognate with Old English nicor, Danish nøk, nøkke, Old Danish jucker, Norwegian nykk, Icelandic nykr, and Dutch nik

From Old Swedish *nædher, *næþer, from Old Norse naðr (“adder, snake in general”), from Proto-Germanic *nadrǭ (“adder, snake in general”). Cognate to Icelandic naður (“adder”). Compare English adder (“viper”) vs deaf adder (“slowworm”).

Feminine form of näder. From Old Norse naðra, feminine form of naðr (“adder, snake in general”), from Proto-Germanic *nadrǭ (“adder, snake in general”). Cogngate to Icelandic naðra, feminine form of naður (“adder”). Compare English adder (“viper”) vs deaf adder (“slowworm”).
From Old Swedish næmna, from Old Norse nefna, nemna, from Proto-Germanic *namnijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.

parole.significato: to have the heart or conscience to do something unpleasant or hurtful.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nænnas, nænna, from Old Norse nenna, from Proto-Germanic *nanþijaną. Cognate to Danish nænne and Icelandic nenna.
From Old Norse nær, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz, comparative of *nēhw. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).

Derived from Old Swedish när (“near”, adverb), from Old Norse nær (“nearer”, comparative adverb), from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz, comparative of *nēhw. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”). The comparative närmare and superlative närmast are from närmare and närmaster respectively,
From Old Norse næstr, a superlative of ná (“near”), corresponding to Proto-Germanic *nēhwist (“nearest, closest”).

parole.significato: to stitch (together), to sew (quickly and loosely)
parole.testo: From Old Norse nesta, nista (“to pin, nail fast”), from Proto-Germanic *nestjaną, likely related to *natją (“net”).

parole.significato: net; a mesh of string, cord, or rope.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish næt, from Old Norse net, from Proto-Germanic *natją, from Proto-Indo-European *ned- (“to turn, twist, knot”).

parole.significato: a needle, a pin (implement for sewing, crocheting, attaching stuff, etc.; however not for knitting)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nāl, from Old Norse nál, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō.
From Old Swedish nut, not, from Old Norse hnot, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts. The irregular stem vowel change in modern Swedish was due to influence from the plural form.

parole.significato: cattle, especially in compounds such as nötkreatur (“cattlebeast”, cf. English neatbeast), or nötkött (“beef”)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nø̄t, from Old Norse naut, from Proto-Germanic *nautą, from Proto-Indo-European *newd- (“to acquire, make use of”).

parole.significato: Added to adjectives to yield their opposites; un-
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ō-, from Old Norse ú-, ó-, from Proto-Germanic *un-, from the Proto-Indo-European *n̥- whence also Greek α- (a-) and English un-.

parole.significato: and; used to connect two homogeneous (similar) words or phrases
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ock, ok, from Old Norse ok, unstressed variant of Proto-Germanic *auk (“also”). Cognate with Norwegian, Danish and Icelandic og, Dutch ook, German auch, and English eke. The unusual spelling with the digraph ch may have been to avoid confusion with the now dated ock (“too, also”).
From Old Swedish oker, uker, from Old Norse ókr, okr, from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz. Cognate of Norwegian åger, Danish åger, German Wucher, Dutch woeker, English oker, Gothic 𐍅𐍉𐌺𐍂𐍃 (wōkrs).

parole.significato: of inherited (land) property rights (of the noun); allodial, especially from time immemorial
parole.testo: From Old Swedish oþol, oþal, odhel, from Old Norse óðal, from Proto-Germanic *ōþalą. Cognate with Danish and Norwegian Bokmål odel, Norwegian Nynorsk odal, Faroese and Icelandic óðal. Compare odel (“soil”), odling (“cultivation”), odla (“to cultivate”).
From Old Norse oft, from Proto-Germanic *ufta.
From Old Norse ok, from Proto-Germanic *juką, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm. Doublet of zygot.
From Old Swedish okunnogher, from Old Norse úkunnigr, from Proto-Germanic *unkunþīgaz, equivalent to o- + kunnig.
From Old Norse úlíkr, from Proto-Germanic *ungalīkaz. By surface analysis, o- + lik. Compare English unlike, Dutch ongelijk, Faroese ólíkur, German ungleich, Norwegian Bokmål ulik.

From Old Norse um, from Proto-Germanic *umbi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi. * As a conjunction, um superseded or blended with Old Norse ef and em, taking on their function as well. This is from Proto-Germanic *jabai (“when, if”), whence also English if and German ob. Doublet of jäv, direct desc

parole.significato: a round (stage of some greater whole)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish umganger, from Old Norse umgangr, from Proto-Germanic *umbigangaz, equivalent to om + gång.
From Old Swedish orþ, from Old Norse orð, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”).

parole.significato: the strength or power to do something
parole.testo: Deverbative of orka (“to have strength”), from Old Norse orka, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”).

parole.significato: to have strength, will, or stamina enough
parole.testo: From Old Swedish orka, from Old Norse orka, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (English work), from Proto-Indo-European *wṛǵ-·.

parole.significato: serpent, snake, or therof slithering legless animal (cf. kopparorm, “slowworm”, sandorm, “sandworm” in the book series…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ormber (“snake/dragon, worm/vermin, ringworm”), from Old Norse ormr, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis, *wrmo- (“serpent, scorpion, maggot, worm”), maybe from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn = slither?”). Akin to English worm, wyrm. Doublet of vurm.
From Old Norse óréttr, from Proto-Germanic *unrehtaz. By surface analysis, o- + rätt.
From Old Norse oss, from Proto-Germanic *uns, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥smé.
From Old Swedish oster, from Old Norse ostr, from Proto-Germanic *justaz, from Proto-Indo-European *yéwHs.
Inherited from Old Swedish ovan, from Old Norse ofan, from Proto-Germanic *ubanē. Cognate with Danish oven and German oben, as well as with the compound forms Dutch boven and English above.

parole.significato: bad weather, usually with heavy precipitation and strong winds; a storm; bad weather
parole.testo: From Old Norse úveðr, óveðr, from Proto-Germanic *unwedrą. Equivalent to o- + väder. Compare English unweather.

parole.significato: an ox (adult castrated male of cattle, typically used as a beast of burden)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish oxe, from Old Norse oxi, uxi, from Proto-Germanic *uhsô, from Proto-Indo-European *uksḗn (“bull”).
From Old Norse panna, from Proto-Germanic *pannǭ.
From Old Norse peningr and pengr. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *panningaz.
From Old Norse penningr, from Proto-Germanic *panningaz. Cognate with English penny.

parole.significato: to peck, to pick (of a bird, or with a pointed instrument)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish pikka, from Old Norse, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną. Compare English pick.
Inherited from Old Swedish pīker, from Old Norse pík, from Proto-Germanic *pīkaz.
From Old Norse plagg, from Proto-Germanic *plaggą.
From Old Swedish plokka, plukka, from Old Norse, from Proto-Germanic *plukkōną. Compare English pluck.
From Old Norse plógr, from Proto-Germanic *plōgaz, *plōguz.

parole.significato: to plow, to plough (soil, or with similar sense extensions to English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish plø̄ghia, from Old Norse plœgja, from Proto-Germanic *plōgijaną.
From Old Norse pottr (“pot, tub, basin”), from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar, tub”). Doublet of potta.
From Old Swedish pund, from Old Norse pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą, from Latin pondo.

parole.significato: to lightly push (apply force to an object to as to make it move)
parole.testo: From Old Norse pota, from Proto-Germanic *putōną.

parole.significato: to (cause to) stream out (with a hissing sound) (of some gas, for example air from a balloon)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish pysa, from Old Norse *pýsa, from Proto-Germanic *pusjaną, from *pus- (“swelling, bladder”), ultimately from the same root as pusta (“to puff”).

parole.significato: a bag (soft container open at the top, usually made of paper, plastic, or fabric)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish posi, from Old Norse posi, from Proto-Germanic *pusô.

parole.significato: a puddle, a pool of water
parole.testo: From Old Norse pœla, pollr, from Proto-Germanic *pōlaz.

parole.significato: a row; a line of entries in a table, or a line of objects
parole.testo: From Old Norse rǫð, from Proto-Germanic *radō (“row”).

parole.significato: coarse fur, bristles (hair of an animal, especially unordered, wild, rugged, shaggy hair)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rǫgg, from Proto-Germanic *rūhaz (“coarse, rough”). Same as Danish rag, Icelandic rogg, Norwegian ragg, Old English adjective raggig and English noun rag, Icelandic rýja (“to rip the wool from sheep, to shear”), Latin ruo (“to rip, dig”) and rutrum (“a shovel”). In older times, wool w
From Old Norse hrapa, from Proto-Germanic *hrapaną, *hrappa- (“fast”), from Proto-Indo-European *krb(ʰ)- (“quickly”).

parole.significato: a race (a large group of individuals of the same species set apart from others on the basis of a common heritage), a br…
parole.testo: From Old Norse rás (“race”), from Proto-Germanic *rēsō.

parole.significato: a break (rest or pause, usually from work)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rǫst, from Proto-Germanic *rastō, *rastijō (“rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *ros-, *res-, *erH- (“rest”).
From Old Norse hrata, from Proto-Germanic *hratt- (“to rush”); see *hradaz (“hasty, quick”). Cognate with Icelandic hrata (“to lose balance”) and Old English hratian (“to hurry”).
From Old Swedish ræghn, from Old Norse regn, from Proto-Germanic *regną.
Old Norse regna, from Proto-Germanic *regnōną, verbal form of *regną (“rain”)
From Old Norse regnbogi (“rainbow”), from Proto-Germanic *regnabugô.
From Old Norse *regndropi, from Proto-Germanic *regnadrupô. Equivalent to regn + droppe.
From Old Swedish räghnogher, reghnogher, from Old Norse *regnugr, from Proto-Germanic *regnagaz (“rainy”), equivalent to regn + -ig.
From Old Norse hreinn (“clean”), from Proto-Germanic *hrainiz.

parole.significato: to remove undesired things (from something); to clean (out), to clear (out), to purge, to wipe, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rēnsa, rænsa, from Old Norse hreinsa, from Proto-Germanic *hrainisōną.
From Old Norse reip, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *raipą, *raipaz, from Proto-Indo-European *roypnós (“strap, band, rope”).

parole.significato: to cause to become upright; to erect
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rēsa, from Old Norse reisa, from Proto-Germanic *raizijaną.
From Old Norse reita, from Proto-Germanic *wraitijaną.
From Old Norse reifa, from Proto-Germanic *raibōną. Compare Old English ārāfian (“uncoil; wind off”), Faroese reiva (“swaddle”).
From rev (“rib”) + ben (“bone”), from Old Swedish rif (+ bēn), from Old Norse rif, from Proto-Germanic *ribją. Doublet of ribba.

parole.significato: to ride (as on a horse or other mount – compare åka)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish riþa, from Old Norse ríða, from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną.

From Old Swedish rīker, from Old Norse ríkr, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz, a derivative of Proto-Germanic *rīks (“king, ruler”), itself a borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs.
From Old Norse ríki, from Proto-Germanic *rīkiją, from Proto-Germanic *rīks, an early borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs. Cognate with Dutch rijk and German Reich.

parole.significato: wealth, riches (of money, possessions, or more generally)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rīkedōmber, rīkdōmber, from Old Norse ríkdómr, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijadōmaz, equivalent to rik + -dom. Compare English richdom.
From Old Norse rím, from Proto-Germanic *rīmą.

parole.significato: ring; a circular piece of material
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ringer, from Old Norse hringr, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz.

parole.significato: to ring; to make a bell produce a sound
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ringia, ringa, from Old Norse hringja, from Proto-Germanic *hringijaną. Cognate with Danish ringe, Norwegian ringe or ringa, Old English hringan, English ring.
From Old Swedish rinna, from Old Norse rinna, from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną.
Inherited from Old Norse hrista, from Proto-Germanic *hristijaną. Cognate of Icelandic hrista.

parole.significato: to draw (usually simpler, more line-based pictures or drawings – compare teckna)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hrīta, from Old Norse hríta, from Proto-Germanic *hrītaną (“to draw, to scratch”).
From Old Swedish rīva, from Old Norse rífa, from Proto-Germanic *rīfaną.

parole.significato: to row; to transport oneself in a small boat, with help of oars
parole.testo: From Old Norse róa, from Proto-Germanic *rōaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁-.
From Old Norse *rukka, rugga, from Proto-Germanic *rukkōną.

From Old Swedish rughn, romn, from Old Norse hrogn, from Proto-Germanic *hrugnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“frogspawn”); cognate with Danish and Norwegian rogn, Icelandic hrogn, German Rogen, and English roe.
From Old Swedish rōpa, from Old Norse hrópa, from Proto-Germanic *hrōpaną. Cognate with Faroese rópa, Icelandic hrópa, Danish råbe, Norwegian rope.

From Old Swedish rosa, from Old Norse hrósa, from the same root as hróðr (“praise”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōþrą. Cognate with Danish rose. Compare German Ruhm (“glory”), Gothic 𐌷𐍂𐍉𐌸𐌴𐌹𐌲𐍃 (hrōþeigs, “glorious”). Related to berömma.
From Old Swedish rost, from Old Norse *rustr, from Proto-Germanic *rustaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

parole.significato: root; the part of a plant that anchors the plant body
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rōt, from Old Norse rót, from Proto-Germanic *wrōts, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds.
From Old Swedish russ, from Old Norse hross, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers-. Doublet of horse and kärra; related to karriär.

parole.significato: to yank, to jerk, to pull quickly
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish rykka, rykkia, from Old Norse rykkja, from Proto-Germanic *rukkijaną. Doublet of rucka.

parole.significato: back; the rear of the body; especially the part between the neck and the end of the spine
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rygger, from Old Norse hryggr, from Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krewk.
From Old Swedish riūka, from Old Norse rjúka, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. See also rök.

parole.significato: to hold (a certain volume of space)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rȳma, from Old Norse rýma, from Proto-Germanic *rūmijaną. Related to rum (“room”).

From Old Norse hrjósa, from Proto-Germanic *hreusaną (“to shudder, shiver, quiver”), from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“raw meat, fresh blood”). Related to Old Norse hrār (“raw, fresh, juicy”), Old English hrēaw, hrēow (“raw”), Avestan 𐬑𐬭𐬏𐬭𐬀 (xrūra, “bloody, gruesome, cruel”), Avestan 𐬑𐬭𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬥𐬙 (xruu
From Old Swedish riūta, rȳta, from Old Norse hrjóta, from Proto-Germanic *hreutaną.

parole.significato: to stretch out (some body part) in some direction (without handing something over or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rækkia, from Old Norse rekja, from Proto-Germanic *rakjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵéyeti.
From Old Swedish rǣdder, from the past participle of Old Swedish rǣþa (“to frighten”), from Old Norse hræða (past participle hræddr), from Proto-Germanic *hrēdijaną.

parole.significato: a narrow, natural or constructed channel (usually open at the top) that conveys or might convey water (or another liqui…
parole.testo: Probably from Old Norse renna, yielding also Icelandic renna, Norwegian renne, Danish rende; from Proto-Germanic *rannijǭ, Also related to Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌽𐌽𐍉 (rinnō), Old High German rinna (both from *rinnǭ).

parole.significato: to run ((back and forth) in a somewhat wild, hectic, or unruly manner – sometimes hyperbolically)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rænna, Old Norse renna, from Proto-Germanic *rannijaną. Originally causative of rinna.
From Old Swedish rǣtter, rǣter, from Old Norse réttr, from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós. Doublet of rätt.
From Old Norse réttr, from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós. Doublet of rät.
From Old Swedish rǣtta, from Old Norse rétta, from Proto-Germanic *rihtijaną. Akin to rätt + -a.
From Old Swedish rar, from Old Norse hrár, from Proto-Germanic *hrawaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂-.

parole.significato: a yard, a stick, a beam
parole.testo: From Old Norse rá (“sailyard, pole for drying fish”), from Proto-Germanic *rahō, cognate with Middle Low German rā, German Rah.
From Old Norse rá, from Proto-Germanic *raihô, *raihą, cognate to German Rah, Rahe.

From Old Swedish snøþer, from Old Norse snauðr, from Proto-Germanic *snauþuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ksnew-. Cognate of German schnöde, Dutch snood, Old English besnyþþan, Latin novacula. Doublet of snygg and snaggad.

From Old Swedish snøre, from Old Norse snœri, related to Proto-Germanic *nēaną (“to sew”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to spin”). Compare Icelandic snæri, Old English snēr (“string of a musical instrument”).

parole.significato: a parish, a municipality; the geographic area of a state church parish, an administrative unit before the Swedish munic…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sōkn, from Old Norse sókn, from Proto-Germanic *sōkniz.
From Old Swedish sōl, from Old Norse sól, from Proto-Germanic *sōl (“sun”).

From Old Norse sumar (neuter), earlier sumarr (masculine), from Proto-Germanic *sumaraz.
From Old Swedish son, sun, from Old Norse sonr, sunr from Proto-Germanic *sunuz, from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús. Masculine in Late Modern Swedish.

parole.significato: a bolete (type of mushroom – fungus (species or individual) belonging to the Boletales order)

parole.significato: sorrow, sadness (usually due to loss or other misfortune, often someone's death)
parole.testo: From Old Norse sorg, from Proto-Germanic *surgō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry; be ill, suffer”).
From Old Swedish sōt, from Old Norse sót, from Proto-Germanic *sōtą.
From Old Swedish sōt, from Old Norse sótt, from Proto-Germanic *suhtiz.
From Old Swedish sova, from Old Norse sofa, from Proto-Germanic *swefaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swep- (“sleep”). Unrelated to English sofa.
Inherited from Old Swedish spana, from Old Norse *spana, from Proto-Germanic *spananą (“to lure, to entice”). Doublet of spänna. Arguably related more distantly to Ancient Greek σπάω (spáō).

parole.significato: to save, to store for future use
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spara, from Old Norse spara, from Proto-Germanic *sparāną.

parole.significato: to kick; to strike with the foot or leg
parole.testo: From Old Norse sparka, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *spurnaną (“to trample, kick”). Compare Icelandic sparka.
From Old Swedish sparre, from Old Norse sparri, from Proto-Germanic *sparrô.

From Old Norse spíkr, from Proto-Germanic *spīkaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“expand, extend, stretch”).

parole.significato: to spill, accidentally pour out liquid
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spilla, from Old Norse spilla, from Proto-Germanic *spilþijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to sunder, split, rend, tear”).

From Old Swedish spinna, from Old Norse spinna, from Proto-Germanic *spinnaną. Cognate with Faroese spinna, Icelandic spinna, Norwegian Bokmål spinne, Norwegian Nynorsk spinna, spinne, Danish spinde, English spin, Dutch spinnen, German spinnen, German Low German spinnen. Compare Finnish kehrätä.

From Old Norse spori, from Proto-Germanic *spurô.

From Old Swedish springa, from Old Norse springa, from Proto-Germanic *springaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sprenǵʰ-.

parole.significato: something that emits a jet of liquid (or several); a sprayer, a squirt
parole.testo: From Old Norse sprúta, from Proto-Germanic *spreutaną.

parole.significato: to blow up, to blast (make (something) explode)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sprængia, from Old Norse sprengja, from Proto-Germanic *sprangijaną, causative of Proto-Germanic *springaną. Doublet of springa.

parole.significato: to throw up, to puke, to vomit
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spȳia, spȳa, spȳ, from Old Norse spýja, from Proto-Germanic *spīwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ptyēw- (“to spit, vomit”). Compare Norwegian and Danish spy, Icelandic spýja, English spew, Dutch spuwen, German speien.

parole.significato: to tighten, to tense (make tense or taut, of muscles, a rope, a spring, or the like)

From Old Swedish spänne, from Old Norse spenni, from the verb spenni (“to stretch”), from Proto-Germanic *spannijaną, cognate with Danish spænde.

parole.significato: stop, catch, block, blockade, ban, limit, bar, lock (something stopping or hindering)
parole.testo: From Old Norse sperra, from Proto-Germanic *sparrijaną.
From Old Norse sparri, from Proto-Germanic *sparrô (“log, wooden beam”).

parole.significato: to foretell, to divine; to tell the future and fortune through supernatural means
parole.testo: From Old Norse spá (“to foretell, prophesy”), from Proto-Germanic *spahōną, *spēhōną (“to observe”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).

parole.significato: a trail or trace; a mark left by something that has passed along or happened, also figuratively
parole.testo: From Old Norse spor, from Proto-Germanic *spurą.

parole.significato: a stack (e.g. of hay), a pile (e.g. of manure)

Inherited from Old Swedish stag, from Old Norse stag, from Proto-Germanic *stagą.

From Old Norse stari, from Proto-Germanic *staraz, from Proto-Indo-European *storo- (“starling”) or *(s)tern- (“starling”), same ultimate source as Old Prussian starnite (“gull”).

parole.significato: strong (capable of producing great physical force)

Old Norse stikka, from Proto-Germanic *stikkô, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg-, related to Etymology 2 below. Compare Icelandic stika, English stick.

From Old Swedish stinga, from Old Norse stinga, from Proto-Germanic *stinganą. Compare Icelandic and Faroese stinga, English sting.

parole.significato: to tip over, to topple (usually a vessel containing a liquid)

From Old Swedish stiærna, from Old Norse stjarna, from Proto-Germanic *sternǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.

From Old Swedish stōþ, from Old Norse stóð, from Proto-Germanic *stōdą. Compare Icelandic stóð.

parole.significato: a log (trunk of a dead tree)

From Old Swedish stōl, from Old Norse stóll, from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *stāl- (“frame, rack, stand”).
From Old Swedish stolpe, from Old Norse stolpi, from Proto-Germanic *stulpô, related to *stallaz (“stable, standing, stall”).

From Old Swedish stōr, from Old Norse stórr (“big, large, tall, great”), from Proto-Germanic *stōraz, from Proto-Indo-European *stāro-.

parole.significato: storm; heavy winds or weather associated with storm winds.

From Old Swedish strand, from Old Norse strǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *strandō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)trAnt-.
Inherited from Old Norse stríða, from Proto-Germanic *strīdaną

parole.significato: to strike (out), to erase, to delete, to remove (strike out, often figuratively)

From Old Norse strangr, from Proto-Germanic *strangaz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“taut”).

parole.significato: a string (kept or intended to be kept taut, for example on an instrument, bow, or racket)

From Old Norse stubbi, from Proto-Germanic *stubbô.

From Old Norse stútr, from Proto-Germanic *stautōną. Cognate with Danish stud, Norwegian stut, and English stot.

parole.significato: a piece (part of something, a part of a distance)

From Old Swedish stȳra, from Old Norse stýra, from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną.

parole.significato: to splash with scattered drops or a small amount of some liquid, to spatter, to sprinkle

parole.significato: to pant and moan (as after exertion)

From late Old Swedish stydh, from earlier Old Swedish stuþ, stoþ, from Old Norse stoð, stuð, from Proto-Germanic *stuþs, from Proto-Indo-European *stut-. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stew- (“be firm”).
From Late Old Swedish stødhia, from Old Swedish styþia, from Old Norse styðja, from Proto-Germanic *stuþjaną.

From Old Swedish svik, Old Norse svik, from Proto-Germanic *swiką.

parole.testo: From Old Norse svenskr, sœnskr, from Proto-Germanic *swihaniskaz (“Swedish”), from *swihô (“Swede”).

parole.significato: to sweep (move in a sweeping motion)

From Old Norse sveiti, from Proto-Germanic *swait-, *swaitô, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- (“to sweat”), *sweyd-.

parole.significato: to swell (become bigger, especially due to being engorged)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svælla, from Old Norse svella, from Proto-Germanic *swellaną. Compare Icelandic svella, English swell, Low German swellen, Dutch zwellen, German schwellen. Doublet of svalla and svullna.

parole.significato: to starve, to hunger (be the victim of famine or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svælta, from Old Norse svelta, from Proto-Germanic *sweltaną.

parole.significato: -in-law; related through marriage, derives from svåger
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svær, from Old Norse *svær, from Proto-Germanic *swehuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros (“father-in-law”).

parole.significato: a folk legend (usually containing supernatural elements and claiming to be true)

From Old Swedish siäldan, säldan, siällan, from Old Norse sjaldan, Proto-Germanic *seldanē.

parole.significato: harmony, friendship, people (or animals) getting along

From Old Swedish sænkia, from Old Norse sænkva, (Old West Norse søkkva) from Proto-Germanic *sankwijaną.

From Old Swedish þiggia, from Old Norse þiggja (“to receive”), from Proto-Germanic *þigjaną.
From Old Swedish til, from Old Norse til, from Proto-Germanic *til (compare *tilą (“goal”)).

parole.significato: an hour (time period of sixty minutes)

From Old Swedish þing, from Old Norse þing (“assembly, council, business”), from Proto-Germanic *þingą.

parole.significato: tether (for binding cattle to a pole or the like)

parole.significato: pitchfork (a large fork used e.g. to move large quantities of hay)

From Old Swedish tiughu, from Old Norse tuttugu, from Proto-Germanic *twai tigiwiz.

parole.significato: a bull ((adult) uncastrated male of cattle)

parole.significato: a thief (one who carries out theft)

From Old Norse tómr, from Proto-Germanic *tōmaz (“empty”).

parole.testo: From Old Norse varða, from Proto-Germanic *wardō, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to perceive, give heed, be careful”). Cognate with Icelandic varða, English ward.

parole.significato: to provide (professional or informal) medical care (to)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish varþa, vordha, from Old Norse varða, from Proto-Germanic *wardāną. Equivalent to vård + -a.
From Old Swedish varta, from Old Norse varta, from Proto-Germanic *wartǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *wers-.
From Old Norse vátr, from Proto-Germanic *wētaz.
From Old Swedish virþa, from Old Norse virða, from Proto-Germanic *wirþijaną.

From Old Swedish vørt, from Old Norse virtr, from Proto-Germanic *wirtiz. Svensk etymologisk ordbok suggests the word is borrowed from Middle Low German. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål vørter, Norwegian Nynorsk vørter, Danish urt.
From Old Norse ynglingr, from Proto-Germanic *jungilingaz.
From Old Swedish yppa, from Old Norse yppa, from Proto-Germanic *uppijaną. Cognate of Danish yppe, Middle Low German uppen, Old English yppan.
From Old Swedish yrkia, from Old Norse yrkja, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną.
From Old Swedish ysta, from Old Norse ysta, from Proto-Germanic *justijaną.
From Old Norse ýtri.
