From Old Swedish ǣgha, from Old Norse eiga, from Proto-Germanic *aigǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *eik-.
From Old Swedish ǣgha, from Old Norse eiga, from Proto-Germanic *aiganą, from Proto-Indo-European *eik-.

parole.significato: an egg (approximately spherical or ellipsoidal body produced by birds, snakes, insects and other animals housing the em…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æg, from Old Norse egg, from Proto-Germanic *ajją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm.
From Old Swedish ælgher, from Old Norse elgr, from Proto-Germanic *algiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élḱis, *h₁ólḱis.

parole.significato: to love (romantically or otherwise – same tone as in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ælska, from Old Norse ælska (Compare Old West Norse elska). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aliskōną (“to care for, cultivate, cherish”).

parole.significato: General term for several child diseases, especially the rickets.
parole.testo: According to Nationalencyklopedins ordbok, the noun definition is attested since 1635, originally meaning "something". The verb comes from the Old Swedish ælta (“to drive, to hunt; to stir, to knead”), from Old Norse elta (“to drive, hunt, knead”), akin to Norwegian Bokmål elte, from Proto-Germanic
From Old Norse elfr, from Proto-Germanic *albī (“river”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål elv, German Elbe.

parole.significato: A human-like creature from Swedish mythology similar to a fairy or elf. She is often a young beautiful female, and can…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ælf, from Old Norse alfr, from Proto-Germanic *albiz (“fairy, elf”).

From Old Swedish æmbete, æmbite, æmbit, æmbeti, from Old Norse embætti, from Proto-Germanic *ambahtiją, whence also ambassad (“embassy”), ambassadör (“ambassador”), amt (“county in Denmark”), German Amt, and Finnish ammatti.
From Old Norse efna, from Proto-Germanic *abnijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃op-, *h₃ep-.
From Old Swedish æfni, from Old Norse efni, from Proto-Germanic *abniją.
From Old Norse enn, from Proto-Germanic *andi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entí.
From Old Norse an, from earlier *þan, from Proto-Germanic *þan. Cognate with English than.
From the oblique case of ände, from Old Swedish ænde, from Old Norse endi, endir, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz.
From Old Swedish ænda, from Old Norse enda, from Proto-Germanic *andijōną.
From Old Norse endir, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos.

parole.significato: a meadow, a field of grass
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æng, from Old Norse eng, from Proto-Germanic *angijō.

parole.significato: a widow (a woman whose husband has died)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ænkia, from Old Norse ekkja (Old East Norse ænkja), from Proto-Germanic *ainakjǭ.
From Old Norse enni, from Proto-Germanic *anþiją.
From Old Norse epli, from Proto-Germanic *apaliją, *apluz (“apple, fruit”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl.

parole.significato: a matter, an errand (purpose of a small trip), an issue, a task, a work item (in a workflow)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ærande, ærinde, ærende, from Old Norse erendi, ørendi, eyrendi (“errand”), from Proto-Germanic *airundiją. Cognate with Danish ærinde, Norwegian ærend, dialectal German Erend and English errand.
From Old Swedish æria, from Old Norse erja, from Proto-Germanic *arjaną.

parole.significato: sleeve; a part of a garment that covers all or part of an arm
parole.testo: From Old Norse ermr, from Proto-Germanic *armijō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erm-i(e)h₂-. See *armaz.

parole.significato: scar (a permanent mark on the skin sometimes caused by the healing of a wound)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ørr, from Proto-Germanic *arwaz.
From Old Swedish ærva, from Old Norse erfa, from Proto-Germanic *arbijaną, equivalent to arv + -a.

parole.significato: box made out of heat-bent wood
parole.testo: From dialectal äska ("little box"), from ask (“box”), from Old Swedish asker, from Old Norse askr, from Proto-Germanic *askaz.

parole.significato: a forge, a furnace, a hearth (a place for heating metal in a blacksmith's shop)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æsia, from Old Norse esja, from Proto-Germanic *asjǭ.
From Old Swedish æta, from Old Norse eta, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-.

parole.significato: a (noble or royal) family, a house
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æt, from Old Norse ætt, from Proto-Germanic *aihtiz.
From Old Swedish æfia (“mud”), from Old Norse efja, from Proto-Germanic *abjǭ (“ebb”). Cognate with Icelandic efja.

parole.significato: a river, a creek, a big stream
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ā, from Old Norse á, from Proto-Germanic *ahwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂.
From Old Norse á, from Proto-Germanic *ana.
From Old Swedish aþra/adher (Old Norse æðr), from Proto-Germanic *ēþrǭ. Cognate with Old English ǣdre, Danish åre, Norwegian åre, German Ader and Dutch ader.
From Old Swedish aþra, adher, from Old Norse æðr, from Proto-Germanic *ēþrō. Cognate with Old English ǣdre, Danish åre, Norwegian åre, German Ader and Dutch ader.

parole.significato: to go by using something more or other than the human or animal body, for example a vehicle, skis, or skates; to go, to…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish aka, from Old Norse aka, from Proto-Germanic *akaną. Cognate with Danish age. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ-. Doublet of agera, which was borrowed from Latin agō, from the same ultimate Proto-Indo-European source.

parole.significato: field; a wide, open space that is used to grow crops
parole.testo: From Old Swedish aker, from Old Norse akr, from Proto-Germanic *akraz (“field”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros (“field”). Akin to English acre.
From Old Swedish āl, from Old Norse áll, from Proto-Germanic *ēlaz.

parole.significato: age; how old something or someone is
parole.testo: From Old Swedish alder, from Old Norse aldr, from Proto-Germanic *aldrą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow”).

parole.significato: to impose a formal requirement (on someone, to do or not do something); to impose, to prescribe, (of a punishment) to i…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish ālæggia, from Old Norse leggja á, from Proto-Germanic *analagjaną. Equivalent to å (“on (obsolete)”) + lägga (“lay”). Cognate with German anlegen, English onlay.
From Old Swedish anger, from Old Norse angr, from Proto-Germanic *angazaz. Compare English anger.
From Old Norse ár, from Proto-Germanic *airō (“oar”). Cognate with Finnish airo.

parole.significato: an ard, an ard plough, a scratch plough
parole.testo: From Old Swedish arþer, from Old Norse arðr, from Proto-Germanic *arþrą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom. Cognate with Icelandic arðr, and Danish, Norwegian, and English ard.

parole.significato: a ridge (long, narrow, not too tall elevation in the landscape)
parole.testo: From Old Norse áss (“rocky ridge”), from Proto-Germanic *amsaz (“shoulder”).
From Old Norse at, from Proto-Germanic *at, from Proto-Indo-European *ád.
From Old Swedish āter, from Old Norse aptr, from Proto-Germanic *aftrą.
From Old Swedish ātta, āta, from Old Norse átta, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōu, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Compare Icelandic átta, Norwegian åtte, Danish otte.
From Old Swedish āttande, āttunde, from Old Norse áttundi, by analogy from earlier átti, from Proto-Germanic *ahtudô.

parole.significato: island, isle (piece of land surrounded by water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish ø, from Old Norse ey, from Proto-Germanic *awjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water”). Cognate with Swedish å (“stream”), English ey (and the initial syllable in island).

parole.significato: to waste, to spend in vain, often used about time
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄þa, from Old Norse eyða, from Proto-Germanic *auþijaną. Cognate with Icelandic eyða, Danish øde, German veröden. Based on the adjective öde (“waste, desolate”) from Old Swedish ø̄þe = Danish øde, Old Saxon ôthi, Old High German ôdi (“empty”), Old Norse auðr (“desolate”).

parole.significato: deserted, desolate, empty (void of people or human activity)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄þe, from Old Norse auðr, from Proto-Germanic *auþijaz.

From phrases of the type det är ödet, where the word has been reinterpreted as the definite article of a neuter noun öde, but is originally the neuter of an obsolete adjective öden, from Old Swedish ø̄þen, from Old Norse auðinn 'destined, fallen to one's lot, granted', formally a participle of an ob
From Old Swedish ø̄gha, from Old Norse auga, from Proto-Germanic *augô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”).
From Old Swedish ø̄ka, from Old Norse auka, from Proto-Germanic *aukaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewg-. Akin to English eke, Danish øge, Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐌺𐌰𐌽 (aukan), Latin augeō.

parole.significato: a beer (a kind or brand of beer)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish öl, from Old Norse ǫl (“ale, beer”), from Proto-Germanic *alu, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elut- (“beer”), or *h₂elu- (“bitter”). Cognate with Icelandic öl. Probably related to Latin alūmen (“alum”); the meaning of "feast" comes from the custom of beer being served at feasts.
From Old Swedish ȳskia, ø̄skia, from Old Norse œskja (“wish”), from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną (“to wish”). The 'n' stems from influence from Middle Low German wunschen. Compare German wünschen.

From Old Swedish ypin, øppin, from Old Norse opinn, from Proto-Germanic *upanaz. Compare Norwegian open, Danish åben, Icelandic opinn, Dutch open, Low German apen, open, German offen, West Frisian iepen, English open.

parole.significato: ear; the part of the body used to hear
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄ra, from Old Norse eyra, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic *ausô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ows-.

parole.significato: a currency unit, one hundredth of a krona (in Denmark, Norway, Sweden)
parole.testo: From Old Norse eyrir, from Proto-Germanic *aurijaz. Potentially related to Latin aureus (“gold coin”), however, according to SAOB not derived from it according to new research. First attested in the 9th to 10th century.

parole.significato: naval, war; pertaining to naval warfare
parole.testo: See örlig (“war”), from Old Norse ørlǫg, from Proto-Germanic *uzlagą. Cognate Dutch oorlog (“war”).
From Old Norse ǫrn, from Proto-Germanic *arô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃or-no- (“eagle”).

From Old Norse urt, oblique case form of Proto-Germanic *wrōts, from Proto-Indo-European *wrd- (“root”). Compare with English wort and the Latin rādīx (“root”). Cognate with the Icelandic rót; Old English rōt (whence Middle English root (“the underground part of a plant”), whence English root).

parole.significato: to scoop (move a fluid, one scoop at a time), pour, serve
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄sa, from Old Norse ausa, from Proto-Germanic *ausaną.
From Old Norse austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą.

parole.significato: east; one of the four major compass points
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄ster, from Old Norse austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą.
From Old Swedish ivir, yvir, ø̄wer, from Runic Swedish ufiR, from Old Norse yfir, from Proto-Germanic *ubiri, from Proto-Indo-European *upéri, from *upér, from *upo.
